sens: Balance or pay of a soldier
Compensation for one who works
What one earns in exchange for a service or work
Figuratively: consequence or retribution attached to an action
G3800.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to military pay, the money given to a soldier for his service. Luke 3:14 shows John the Baptist advising soldiers to be content with their pay, without demanding more.
2. More broadly, it signifies the salary or wages of any worker. In 1 Corinthians 9:7, Paul speaks of the expenses or wages inherent to any legitimate work: the soldier does not equip himself at his own expense, the vine grower does not plant without eating the fruit, the shepherd does not keep the flock without feeding on the milk.
3. It is the just compensation due for a service rendered. In 2 Corinthians 11:8, Paul speaks of the salary he received from other churches for serving them.
4. Figuratively, it is the consequence or moral retribution attached to an action. Romans 6:23 uses it strikingly: "the wages of sin is death" — sin carries its own retribution, just as work carries its wages.
G3800.origine: The word comes from "opsarion" (small fish) and the verb "ōneomai" (to buy, to acquire). Originally, it referred to the money given to buy food — the provision or money for sustenance. The meaning has broadened to denote any salary or compensation. The word thus evokes the fundamental idea: what one receives in exchange for a service, what one needs to live.
G3800.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament. Paul uses it three times: in 1 Corinthians 9:7, he uses it to describe the expenses or sustenance inherent to any legitimate work; in 2 Corinthians 11:8, he refers to it as the salary he received; in Romans 6:23, he uses it strikingly in a parallelism: the wages of sin (its inevitable consequence) contrasts with the free gift of God (eternal life). Luke 3:14 uses it for military pay. The word pivots between the concrete sense (pay) and the moral sense (retribution).
G3800.portee: This word reminds us that all work deserves compensation, and that God recognizes the service rendered. But above all, Romans 6:23 gives this word a major spiritual significance: sin is not a moral abstraction, it has real and deadly consequences, like a wage one receives. However, the free gift of God in Jesus Christ offers a way of escape. This word helps the Christian take seriously the gravity of sin and the incomparable grace of salvation.

sens: To set a trap, to catch with cunning
Figuratively, to catch someone off guard by putting them in an impossible position
G3802.detail:
1. The base word means to set a trap or net to capture prey: it is the concrete image of a hunter setting a trap. In Matthew 22:15, the Pharisees seek to "surprise" Jesus, that is, to put him in difficulty by asking him a crafty question — just as one would set a net for game.

2. Figuratively, "to surprise" means to catch someone off guard, to confuse them or put them in a situation from which they cannot escape. The Pharisees hope that Jesus' words will provide them with a reason to accuse him: they want to "surprise him with his own words."
G3802.origine: The word comes from the Greek παγίς (pagís), which denotes a trap or net set to capture game. The verb παγιδεύω adds the idea of action: it is to set the trap, to cause to fall into the trap. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew נָקַשׁ (naqash, "to set a trap") and יָקֹשׁ (yaqosh, "to cause to fall into a trap").
G3802.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament. Matthew uses it to describe the tactic of the Pharisees towards Jesus after he has raised the question of the tribute due to Caesar (Matthew 22:15). Jesus' adversaries consciously seek him — they "consult together" — with the intention of defeating him with his own words. The context indicates that this is not an accident, but a premeditated calculation: they set a net of words.
G3802.portee: This word reveals the attitude of Jesus' enemies: they are not sincere contradictors, but walking traps. For the reader, it invites one to see that the true intentions of the adversaries of the Gospel are often not what they seem — they hide a calculation. It is also an invitation to vigilance: in the Christian life, one can be "surprised" by subtle traps, temptations that present themselves under the guise of respectability or reason.

sens: Device or net used to capture animals or to catch someone by surprise
Figuratively, a situation or word that deceives and leads to the downfall of one who falls into it
Temptation or desire that diverts from good and leads to destruction
Cunning or scheme of the devil to enslave souls
G3803.detail:
1. In the concrete sense, a trap is a capturing device — net, snare, or noose — that catches the animal or person who is lacking vigilance. Luke 21:35 uses it to describe how the day of Judgment will come like a net upon all the inhabitants of the earth: suddenly, inevitably, without one being able to avoid it.
2. The figurative trap is any word, situation, or event that misleads and causes spiritual ruin. Romans 11:9 speaks of the table of Israel becoming a trap — what was meant to nourish (the promises of God) has turned into an obstacle and an occasion for falling.
3. It is also the temptation that leads to evil and loss. In 1 Timothy 6:9, wanting to get rich at all costs is a trap: the desire for wealth ensnares one in ruin and destruction.
4. Finally, the trap is the scheme of the devil to enslave. In 2 Timothy 2:26, the devil captures men in his traps to bend them to his will — an image of spiritual domination from which one can escape.
G3803.origine: The Greek word pagis comes from the verb pegnyumi ("to fix, to drive in"), which suggests the action of setting, of laying a trap. In Hebrew, parallel words such as moqesh ("trap"), rèshet ("net"), and pah ("snare") are all concrete in origin. The word refers to the fundamental idea of "what is set" or "what is laid out" to capture.
G3803.emploi: The word pagis appears 5 times in the New Testament, primarily in the pastoral epistles and in Luke. In Luke, it retains its concrete-figurative sense of the final judgment. In Paul, it takes on spiritual and moral significance: Romans 11:9 applies it to the moral fall of Israel, while the epistles to Timothy link it to the devil's cunning and material temptations (wealth, pride). The pastoral context shows a concern for Christians exposed to spiritual seductions and traps.
G3803.portee: This word warns the believer against two realities: the subtlety of temptations, which never present themselves as evil, and the reality of spiritual warfare. It reminds us that the devil does not act openly, but through traps — flattering words, legitimate desires diverted, false promises — hence the urgency of vigilance and prayer to avoid being ensnared.

sens: What happens to someone: a trial, an affliction
A feeling, a passive emotion, particularly carnal desires or passions
The action of suffering, enduring pain
G3804.detail:
1. This word primarily refers to anything painful that happens to us: suffering, affliction, trial. Paul lists the sufferings he endured in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11). But the Bible mainly uses it for the sufferings of Christ — what He endured for us — and those experienced by Christians who follow Jesus: Paul speaks of "the fellowship of His sufferings" (Philippians 3:10) and how the sufferings of Christ abound in us (2 Corinthians 1:5).
2. The word also refers to an emotion or passion that dominates us, particularly carnal desires: "the passions of sins" that were at work in our members before conversion (Romans 7:5), or the "passions of the flesh" that believers have crucified (Galatians 5:24).
3. Finally, it is the very act of suffering, enduring: Jesus was "made perfect through sufferings" (Hebrews 2:10), meaning He was made complete and perfect through what He endured.
G3804.origine: This word comes from the verb "pascho" (πάσχω), which literally means "to be affected" or "to be reached" by something. The root expresses the idea of undergoing an action, receiving it passively. In Greek, πάθημα contrasts with active action: while the agent acts, the one who suffers receives. It is a classical Greek word used to express what happens to us from the outside, especially adversity and pain.
G3804.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles of Paul and Peter. It consistently describes the trials of the apostles — Paul lists his persecutions and sufferings (2 Timothy 3:11), and Christians "share" in them just as they do in consolation (2 Corinthians 1:6-7). A decisive usage is that of the sufferings of Christ (1 Peter 1:11, 5:1): it is what Jesus bore for us. Christians are invited to "fellowship" in these sufferings by following Jesus (Philippians 3:10, 1 Peter 4:13). A final, less frequent usage refers to carnal passions, the desires of the flesh (Romans 7:5, Galatians 5:24).
G3804.portee: This word reminds Christians that suffering is never a disgrace, but a communion with Jesus Himself. The sufferings we endure while remaining faithful are not meaningless: they unite us to Him who suffered for us and lead us to share in His glory. This changes everything: suffering becomes the path of the disciple, not a regrettable accident.

sens: One who is called to undergo suffering
One who must experience pain and affliction
G3805.detail:
1. The word refers to a person marked by suffering, to whom suffering is reserved or destined. In Acts 26:23, Paul states that Christ was "destined to suffer" — this is the announcement of His passion, His path to the cross, foretold in the prophecies of the Old Testament.
2. More broadly, it refers to someone who is subjected to suffering, who is bound to it or devoted to it. The word does not describe the suffering itself, but the condition of the one who undergoes it or is its object.
G3805.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "pascho" (πάσχω), which means "to suffer" or "to undergo." The suffix "-tos" forms a passive adjective: one who undergoes the action. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this verb often translates the Hebrew "yatsar" (to suffer, to endure) and appears notably in passages about the suffering Servant of Isaiah. It is a word that speaks to the reality of experienced or inevitable suffering.
G3805.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:23. Paul pronounces it before King Agrippa to describe the inevitable nature of Christ's passion: it is not an accident, but the fulfillment of God's will announced by the prophets. This suffering of Christ is linked to His resurrection and His mission as a light for Israel and the nations.
G3805.portee: This word reminds us that the suffering of Christ is not a defeat, but an assumed and prophesied destiny. For the believer, it affirms that the sufferings of Jesus are part of God's plan and serve our salvation. It is an invitation to see the cross not as an incomprehensible tragedy, but as the fulfillment of what God had announced.

sens: What happens to someone, what they undergo
Violent and uncontrolled emotion, passionate desire
In a biblical sense, a wicked desire that enslaves the soul
G3806.detail:
1. Literally, it is what "happens" to a person, what they "undergo" — like suffering or an event that seizes us without our control. It is a basic word that names the past experience of the body and soul.

2. More specifically, it is a brutal emotion, a violent affection of the soul — a passion in the ancient sense of the word, meaning a force that carries us away against our will. It is unbridled desire, the covetousness that takes hold of us.

3. In the New Testament, this word always refers to a wicked, sinful desire that submits the body and spirit to rebellion. In Romans 1:26, it refers to "vile passions" by which God gives the wicked over to their own slavery. In Colossians 3:5, Paul commands believers to "put to death" the passions that dwell in their members. It is a power of sin, not merely an emotion.
G3806.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to be affected" or "to undergo something." It is very close to "pathēma" (πάθημα), which also designates the experience undergone, but "passion" emphasizes more the passive and uncontrolled nature of desire. It is a passive word: the one who undergoes it does not govern it; they are its victim. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it primarily translates mourning and suffering, but in classical Greek, it also encompasses violent emotions.
G3806.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always to describe a wicked desire. In Romans 1:26, it qualifies the "vile passions" that drive humans to sexual immorality: God does not create them; He "gives them over," meaning He abandons sinners to the power of their own covetousness. In Colossians 3:5, Paul groups passion with impurity and greed as "members" to be put to death — habits of the old self that have no place in the believer. In 1 Thessalonians 4:5, it opposes temperance: not to indulge in "passionate lust" means to master one's carnal desire by grace. Everywhere, it is an enemy of sanctification.
G3806.portee: This word helps the believer understand that sin is not primarily an intellectual transgression, but an enslavement of desire: we undergo passion even before we choose it. Passion is a power that chains us. But the Gospel announces that Christ liberates: the believer who dies to sin with Christ can "put to death" their passions (Colossians 3:5) by grace and prayer. It is an invitation to move from slavery to freedom.

sens: Slave responsible for supervising and educating the children of a wealthy family
Guide who trains and leads
The Law seen as a tutor leading to Christ
G3807.detail:
1. In wealthy Greek and Roman households, the pedagogue was a trusted slave who accompanied the children to school, supervised them, and instructed them in good morals — it was not the master who taught the letters, but an educator responsible for their conduct. Paul speaks of this to distinguish himself from a pedagogue: he tells the Corinthians that he is not just another teacher, but a spiritual father, since he is the one who has begotten them in Christ (1 Corinthians 4:15).
2. More broadly, the term refers to any person or force that guides and leads someone toward a destination, training and preparing them.
3. Paul calls the Law a "pedagogue" (Galatians 3:24-25): like the slave who led the child to school, the Law has led us to Christ, showing us our sin and our need for grace. But once we have come to faith in Christ, we no longer need it — we have become spiritually mature.
G3807.origine: The Greek word comes from "paîs" (child) and "ágô" (I lead). It literally designates one who leads children. In Greek, it is clearly opposed to didáskalos (schoolmaster): the pedagogue educated in a broad sense, while the master taught knowledge. This term, borrowed from Greek customs, allowed Paul to express the idea that the Law plays a temporary guiding role, not a permanent master.
G3807.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Paul’s writings. In 1 Corinthians 4:15, Paul uses it to set himself apart: by saying "you do not have many fathers" in the face of many "teachers" in Christ, he asserts that he is much more than a pedagogue — he is a spiritual father. In Galatians 3:24-25, he develops a major theological image: the Law acts as a pedagogue that keeps us and leads us to Christ, after which its function ends. This image illustrates the transition from the old covenant to the new, from the status of minors under guardianship to that of adult heirs.
G3807.portee: This image of the pedagogue sheds light on the transition that believers experience: the Law is not bad; it has a vital pedagogical role, but it is not the final destination. It convinces us of sin and prepares us for faith in Christ. Once in Christ, we enter into a new relationship, no longer that of children under supervision, but of adopted sons and daughters. This reminds us that each stage of spiritual life has its function, and that growing sometimes means freeing oneself from a temporary guardianship to move freely toward the one who has redeemed us.

sens: young male child, toddler
child, young man in a broader sense
G3808.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a small boy, a young child — literally a "little" boy, as it is a diminutive form. The classic example is the little boy who offers his five barley loaves and two fish to Jesus (John 6:9), a modest yet touching contribution that will miraculously be sufficient to feed the multitude.
2. In common usage of the time, the word gradually loses its diminutive nuance and can more broadly refer to a child or a young man — not just a very young child, but a child or adolescent in general.
G3808.origine: The Greek word παιδάριον is formed by diminutive of παῖς (pais), which means "child" or "boy." This diminutive suffix gives a sense of smallness or tenderness. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word generally renders the Hebrew נַעַר (naaʿar), which designates a young boy or adolescent.
G3808.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 6:9, in the account of the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves. It refers to the young boy who offers his provisions to Jesus — a scene where the humility and generosity of this child become the instrument of the miracle. Its unique use in this context shows the narrator's tenderness for this anonymous character whose faith and simple gesture play a central role in the narrative.
G3808.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus values every person, even the youngest, and that no act of faith or generosity is ever too small for God. The little boy becoming the vessel of a miracle teaches the reader that the greatness of the Kingdom depends not on size or human importance, but on the disposition of the heart to serve.

sens: education of a child
instruction, teaching
punishment, corrective discipline
G3809.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the complete education of a child: the entire process that shapes and prepares him for life, under the guidance of a parent or teacher (Ephesians 6:4 speaks of raising children "by correcting and instructing them").
2. More broadly, any teaching and instruction — that by which one learns and progresses spiritually or morally. This is why Scripture is said to be "useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16).
3. In particular, the correction that comes from a legitimate authority — a father, or God himself — to restore one who has gone astray. It is a form of love: Hebrews 12:7 affirms that punishment shows that God treats you "as sons," and Hebrews 12:11 promises that "every punishment" ultimately yields "the peaceful fruit of righteousness."
G3809.origine: The word comes from the verb paideuô (to train, educate, correct) and the noun paîs (child). Its starting image is therefore the action of raising a child. In ancient Greek, the word encompasses the entire educational process. In the Greek Old Testament, it mostly translates the Hebrew word mousâr, which refers to both instruction and corrective punishment — the idea being that pedagogy and discipline are not separated.
G3809.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, always in educational or disciplinary contexts. In Paul’s writings (Ephesians 6:4, 2 Timothy 3:16), it refers to instruction and correction as means of shaping the Christian. In the letter to the Hebrews (12:5, 7, 8, 11), it specifically applies to God’s discipline of His spiritual children: God disciplines because He loves, and this discipline bears fruit of righteousness. The word thus navigates between three related meanings: general education, specific instruction, and corrective punishment — the author shows that these three aspects are part of the same formation process.
G3809.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals that God acts as a father: He educates, instructs, and corrects those who are His children. The difficulties and corrections of the Christian life are not accidents, but marks of divine affection. The word also frees from guilt: correction comes from an intention of love and progress, not from rejection. It is a call to see discipline as a blessing, not as arbitrary punishment.

sens: one who teaches, instructs
one who corrects through discipline
G3810.detail:
1. The teacher is one who teaches and instructs: Paul refers to the master who possesses knowledge and communicates it to others. In Romans 2:20, Paul describes the Jew as "the teacher of the foolish," one who claims to guide those who do not know the law. It is the image of someone who has received training and transmits it.
2. The teacher is also one who corrects and disciplines: this is a less obvious but equally biblical sense. In Hebrews 12:9, the word refers to fathers who chastise us — they educate us not only through teaching but also through correction and rebuke that shape us. This sense shows that biblical education is not soft: it includes discipline.
G3810.origine: The word comes from the verb παιδεύω (paideuô), which means to teach, educate, correct. The root παῖς (pais) evokes the child, the person who learns. In biblical Hebrew, the word מוּסָר (mûsar, discipline, correction) often translates this idea. The teacher is thus literally one who educates the child — not only through lessons but through a comprehensive training that shapes character.
G3810.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament: in Romans 2:20 and Hebrews 12:9. In Romans, Paul uses it somewhat ironically when he speaks of the Jew who considers himself a teacher of those who are ignorant of the law. It is a title of intellectual and spiritual authority. In Hebrews, the meaning shifts towards correction: the fathers who chastise us act as teachers, in the sense that they shape us through discipline. Both uses show that in biblical thought, teaching and correction are two facets of the same education.
G3810.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand that true education — that of God towards His children — is never purely theoretical. It involves correction and discipline, not just instruction. This helps to accept with gratitude the trials and rebukes from God: they are not arbitrary punishments, but acts of a Father who shapes and teaches us.

sens: To train and instruct someone, especially a child, through teaching
To correct, punish, or rectify someone through chastisements or trials
To correct with discipline in order to lead to obedience and wisdom
G3811.detail:
1. To instruct and train: the word primarily denotes the action of teaching and cultivating the mind, as one does with children. Moses "was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22), and the grace of God "teaches us to renounce ungodliness" (Titus 2:12). It is a learning process that shapes the person.
2. To chastise and correct: the word is also used to denote blows, rods, or sufferings sent for correction. Jesus says He will release the prisoner "after having him beaten with rods" (Luke 23:16). The Lord "chastises" those He loves, as a father corrects his son (Hebrews 12:7).
3. To correct through trial: these two meanings unite in the idea of a benevolent correction that instructs. God "chastises" His own to train them in righteousness and wisdom, not out of mere anger, but as a discipline of love that leads to obedience.
G3811.origine: The word comes from παῖς (paîs), "child," and evokes the action of training and raising a child. In Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, it often translates יָסַר (yassar), which means "to correct, to punish" — an image of adjustment and setting in order. The root expresses the idea of discipline: that which educates by correcting, by inflicting useful suffering. This is why the word encompasses both gentle instruction and severe correction.
G3811.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Epistles and Revelation. In the sense of "to teach or instruct," it is found in Luke and Paul: Moses instructs in Egypt (Acts 7:22), grace teaches us to renounce evil (Titus 2:12), and Hymenaeus must learn through chastisement not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). In the sense of "to chastise or correct," it first refers to the sufferings inflicted on Jesus before His crucifixion (Luke 23:16, 22), then to divine discipline: the Lord chastises those He loves, as a father does his son (Hebrews 12:6-7, 10), in order to train them in righteousness (2 Timothy 2:25). In 1 Corinthians 11:32 and Revelation 3:19, it expresses God's merciful correction that punishes His children so that they may not be lost. The term thus unites education and corrective judgment.
G3811.portee: This word reveals that divine discipline is never blind vengeance, but a form of love. When God chastises, He shapes and educates, like a father who corrects for the good of his child. For the Christian, this means that the trials and corrections he endures can be means by which God shapes him towards righteousness and wisdom. It is an invitation to see discipline not as a distant punishment, but as a proof of paternal love that corrects and sanctifies us.

sens: From the moment one was a child, since childhood
G3812.detail: 1. The word denotes the moment when something began, going back to the person's childhood. In Mark 9:21, the father explains that his son's illness has been present "from childhood": it did not come suddenly, but has accompanied the child since his earliest years. It is a way of saying "for a long time, since very little."
G3812.origine: The word is formed from *paidióthen*, which comes from *paídion* (child) and the ending *-then* which indicates the starting point, the origin in time or space ("from"). It is a classical expression to say "from childhood": it combines the idea of youth with the idea of a duration that goes back far.
G3812.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in ancient Greek: Mark 9:21. The father of the boy afflicted with a mute spirit uses it in response to Jesus' question. He wants to show the long-standing and deep nature of the illness, suggesting that this evil has been rooted in his son's life very early on, perhaps since his birth or his earliest days. This underscores the gravity of the situation.
G3812.portee: This detail reveals a parent's anguish in the face of long-term suffering: when the illness is inscribed "from childhood," it has marked the entire existence, it is not a passing incident. It also helps to understand why the father deemed it good to bring his son to Jesus and why he hopes for an extraordinary intervention: only an act of divine power can break such an ancient curse.

sens: A young child, very young, generally an infant or a toddler
A slightly older child, but still in childhood
An affectionate or familiar term to address someone, even an adult
G3813.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a very young child, an infant or a small child, the image of a small, fragile, and dependent person. This is how it is used for the little Jesus whom the Magi come to worship in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:8), or for the child John the Baptist who grows up (Luke 1:80), or for the newborn Moses hidden by his parents (Hebrews 11:23). 2. The word also extends to older children, those who run and play in the streets, or whom Jesus calls to him by saying, "Let the little children come to me" (Mark 10:14) and taking them in his arms (Mark 9:36). 3. In conversation, the word becomes a familiar way to address someone with tenderness or friendliness, as Jesus says to the disciples on the shore: "Children, do you have any food?" (John 21:5), or as John writes to the young Christians in his church: "I write to you, little children, because you know the Father" (1 John 2:18).
G3813.origine: The word comes from a root that means "small" or "diminished" — it is a diminutive form of the Greek word παῖς (paîs), which can mean child or young servant. This diminutive indicates affection, tenderness, as when one says in French "ma petite" or "mon petit" to speak gently. In Hebrew, this word often translates יֶלֶד (yéled), which literally means "one who is born," or נַעַר (nahar), which designates a young boy.
G3813.emploi: The word appears 49 times in the New Testament, especially in the four Gospels and the letters of John. In Matthew and Luke, it is very common to speak of Jesus as a child (Matthew 2:8-14, Luke 2:17-40) and of the children that people brought to Jesus for him to bless (Mark 10:13-14, Luke 18:15-17). Mark also uses it for Jairus's daughter whom Jesus raises (Mark 5:39-41) or for the convulsing child (Mark 9:24-37). John uses it in the symbolic Revelation — a woman in labor gives birth to a child (John 16:21) — and in the affectionate tone of the pastor addressing his disciples (John 21:5, 1 John 2:13, 2:18). Paul uses it once to urge the Corinthians to leave childishness in their faith (1 Corinthians 14:20). The word always carries a nuance of tenderness or vulnerability.
G3813.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus experienced childhood, smallness, dependence — he was that fragile "little child" of Bethlehem. It also shows us how Jesus sees the child: not as an insignificant being, but as a model of trust and simplicity before God (Mark 10:14-15). For our Christian life, this speaks to us of a form of childlike trust in our Heavenly Father, far from arrogance.

sens: young girl
young woman serving in a household
female slave
condition of slavery (figurative sense)
G3814.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a young girl or young woman. It is the diminutive of the Greek word παῖς (child, servant), which suggests the idea of youth and subordination.
2. The female servant is a young woman who works in a household, often of modest means. In the four Gospels, it is female servants who accuse Peter of being with Jesus: one approaches him in Matthew 26:69, another sees him near the fire in Luke 22:56, female servants call out to him in Mark 14:66 and 14:69, and in John 18:17. They are ordinary domestics, attentive to comings and goings.
3. The word can also refer to a slave in the strict sense: a woman who belongs to someone. In Acts 12:13, Rhoda is a female servant who answers the door of Mary's house; in Acts 16:16, a young slave girl with a spirit of divination brings much profit to her masters through her predictions.
4. In Galatians 4:22-30, Paul uses this word figuratively to speak of Hagar, Abraham's female slave, and contrasts her status with that of Sarah, the free woman. Hagar's slavery becomes the image of the spiritual slavery of those who are under the Law.
G3814.origine: The word is the diminutive of παῖς (child, boy servant, slave). This diminutive form emphasizes youth, and often a certain dependence or social inferiority. In Hebrew and Aramaic, this word translates שִׁפְחָה (shifhah, female servant) and אָמָה (amah, slave or woman of lower status).
G3814.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the New Testament. In the four Gospels, it refers to the female servants who recognize Peter during his denial (Matthew 26:69, Mark 14:66 and 14:69, Luke 22:56, John 18:17): humble women, close to the high priest's house, witnesses to the drama. In Acts, Rhoda is specifically mentioned as a female servant who keeps the door (Acts 12:13), and another slave girl, possessed by a spirit, profits her masters through divination (Acts 16:16). In Galatians, Paul uses the word to recount the story of Hagar, Abraham's female servant (Galatians 4:22, 4:23, 4:30, 4:31), and draws an allegorical lesson: Hagar's slavery symbolizes the slavery of those who remain under the Law, while Sarah and her free son represent freedom in Christ.
G3814.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus spoke to female servants, to humble and often forgotten people. They are witnesses to his arrest and Peter's denial— their perspective matters. Paul, in speaking of Hagar, invites believers to reflect on the difference between slavery and freedom in Christ: not a servitude arising from the Law, but adoption as children of God.

sens: To play like a child, to have fun without serious purpose
To take pleasure in games, dances, songs
To engage in entertainment, often excessively or idolatrously
G3815.detail:
1. The word first evokes childlike play, simple and carefree amusement. In 1 Corinthians 10:7, Paul recounts the behavior of the Israelites in the desert who, after a meal, "rose up to amuse themselves" — that is, they began to dance and celebrate around the golden calf.
2. More broadly, the verb designates entertainment in general: songs, dances, games. It is not merely pleasure, but the noisy and visible expression of shared enjoyment.
3. In the biblical context, the word often takes on a critical tone: entertainment becomes a form of escape, even idolatry, when one forgets God to lose oneself in pleasure. Paul uses it as a warning against this diversion of the heart.
G3815.origine: The word comes from the same root as "παῖς" (paîs), which means "child." Its primary image is that of a child playing freely. In Hebrew, the Bible uses the verbs צָחַק (tsâhaq) and שָׂחַק (sâhaq), which have the same range of meanings: from innocent play to licentious or mocking play. The link with childhood emphasizes that playing is primarily an activity without responsibility or serious purpose.
G3815.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Corinthians 10:7, where Paul cites Exodus and recalls how the Israelites "amused themselves" in worship of the golden calf (Exodus 32:6). It is a pivotal moment: after the idolatrous meal, the people move on to amusements — dance, music, games — as if forgetting God were natural once their bellies were full. Paul uses this memory to warn the Corinthians: do not repeat this same trajectory. The word thus carries the weight of this lesson: amusement that diverts from the Lord is a form of rebellion.
G3815.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine their heart: pleasure and relaxation are not bad in themselves, but they can become idolatry when they lead us away from God. Paul poses the underlying question: to what do we dedicate our joy? To communion with the Lord, or to entertainments that distract us from Him? It is a call to vigilance of the heart in our leisure and celebrations.

sens: young boy or girl, small child
young man or woman, adolescent
servant, slave, attendant
minister or officer in the service of a king
servant of God, one who obeys God
G3816.detail:
1. A small child, boy or girl, generally in early childhood: Herod had the "children" two years old and under killed in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16), and the child Jesus stays in Jerusalem without his parents noticing (Luke 2:43).

2. A young man or woman, older than a small child, often of an age to serve or learn: Jesus raises the daughter of Jairus by saying, "Child, arise" (Luke 8:54), which is addressed to a young girl.

3. A servant, a slave, someone in the service of a master: the centurion tells Jesus, "My servant is paralyzed" (Matthew 8:6, 8), and the Gospel speaks of the "servant" who is healed (Matthew 8:13). A master calls one of his "servants" to find out what is happening (Luke 15:26).

4. A minister or officer of the king, placed under his authority: Herod hears about the miracles of Christ "by his servants" (Matthew 14:2), meaning his court officials.

5. The servant of God, one who fully submits to God: Jesus is called the "servant" of God (Acts 3:13, 26), and David as well (Luke 1:69), as is Israel, the people of God (Luke 1:54).
G3816.origine: The word comes from a Greek root related to the idea of one who is young and learning, or who belongs to someone. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, it mainly translates as "servant" or "young boy," two meanings that often overlapped in the ancient world: a young person had no independence and was naturally under authority. The same Greek word also appears in compounds like "young female servant" (παιδίσκη). It is a common word, at the heart of daily life and authority relationships.
G3816.emploi: The word "child" or "servant" appears 24 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and the Gospels. In the sense of "child," it describes small and young ones: the children that Jesus blesses in the temple (Matthew 21:15), the child Jesus himself (Luke 2:43), and the young girl raised by Jesus (Luke 8:54). In the sense of "servant" or "slave," the word designates the servant of the centurion (Matthew 8:6, 8, 13), the servants of a household (Luke 12:45, 15:26), and also the officers of King Herod (Matthew 14:2). A particular and profound use: Jesus and David are both called the "servant" of God (Acts 3:13; Luke 1:69), and Israel as well (Luke 1:54), borrowing language from the Old Testament. Thus, the word shifts from the concrete (a small child, a household servant) to the spiritual (radical obedience to God).
G3816.portee: This word teaches two major truths. First, it reminds us that childhood is an important biblical reality: Jesus humbles himself to take the form of a child, he touches children, he defends them. Second, it reveals that the highest title is that of "servant of God": Jesus accepts this name, which expresses total submission to the will of the Father. Being a child before God and a servant of God is not a humiliation, but true dignity.

sens: to hit with the hand or fist
to strike with a weapon, especially a sword
to sting, wound (as with a venomous animal)
G3817.detail:
1. To strike someone with the hand or fist: this is the most basic gesture, that of a direct blow delivered up close. In Matthew 26:68 and Luke 22:64, the men holding Jesus ask him to guess who struck him in the face — they strike him with their bare hands, out of contempt and mockery.

2. To strike with a weapon, especially a sword: the blow becomes deadly or seriously injuring. When Peter draws his sword in John 18:10 and Mark 14:47, he "strikes" the servant of the high priest and cuts off his ear — this is an act of armed violence, not a mere slap.

3. To sting or wound, as a venomous animal does: the word applies to the sting of a scorpion in Revelation 9:5, where the locusts of the fifth plague torment men. The blow here is tiny but painful and repeated.
G3817.origine: The Greek verb παίω (paiō) expresses the action of striking in general, from a punch to a weapon blow. It is related to other words describing blows or violent gestures. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it primarily renders the Hebrew נָכָה (nākâh, "to strike, to strike mortally"), a very common word in accounts of battles and divine judgment. The root primarily evokes the physical, raw, and direct gesture.
G3817.emploi: The verb παίω appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in four key passages. Three times it describes the contempt inflicted on Jesus: the two mocking interrogators who strike him (Matthew and Luke), and Peter who strikes out of misplaced zeal (Mark and John — the same event reported twice). Once, it describes the sting of the infernal scorpion (Revelation). The word has no nuanced meaning: it always designates a direct blow, with or without a weapon, but it also applies to the action of living creatures. It is a verb of concrete and brutal action.
G3817.portee: This act of striking summarizes a dark part of the Passion drama: the physical humiliation of Jesus by those who despise him, and Peter's impulsiveness in acting before understanding. Seeing Jesus struck defenseless calls the reader to meditate on his voluntary humiliation and on the pain of the righteous being persecuted. The image of the scorpion that stings also reminds us that inflicted harm, even small blow after blow, can torture and devastate.

sens: in a distant or very remote past
in a recent past or just before
for a considerable time up to the present
G3819.detail:
1. The most common meaning refers to a distant, ancient, bygone past: it expresses the idea that an event occurred a very long time ago. When Jesus says to the cities of Tyre and Sidon, "long ago they would have repented" (Luke 10:13), he implies that these cities would have changed their attitude long ago if they had seen the miracles done among you.
2. In a context of questions or brief description, the word can simply refer to a recent past or a short duration: Pilate asks the centurion if the crucified one had been dead "for a long time" (Mark 15:44), meaning shortly before.
3. The word can qualify a continuous duration up to the present moment, marking that something lasts or extends over a long time: Paul tells the Corinthians, "You have long imagined that we justify ourselves to you" (2 Corinthians 12:19), meaning that a false impression has persisted for some time.
G3819.origine: The word πάλαι comes from a Greek root expressing antiquity and remoteness in time. It often translates the Hebrew אָז ("then," "formerly") in ancient Greek, which refers to a defined and distant past. Its family of words includes adjectives and nouns that express the idea of what is old or ancient. It is a simple and direct word, without diminutive or compound: it designates the past by establishing a clear demarcation line between formerly and now.
G3819.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. Matthew and Luke use it identically to express Jesus' regret (Matthew 11:21, Luke 10:13): these cities would have acted differently "long ago" if they had seen his signs. Mark uses it for an immediate past (Mark 15:44), showing that the word is not limited to distant centuries. Paul and the author of the epistle to the Hebrews use it to mark a contrast between a bygone era and the present time: Hebrews 1:1 speaks of the way "formerly" God spoke to the fathers, to show the transition to revelation in Christ. In 2 Peter 1:9, the adjective "old" qualifies the forgotten sins of the Christian, emphasizing their temporal and spiritual distance.
G3819.portee: This word teaches the Christian reader the importance of seeing how God acts through time. It reminds us that the signs and wonders of Christ had an immediate impact, and that the refusal to believe exposes one to responsibility. It also emphasizes that the distant past — that of the prophets, of forgiven old sins — remains present in God's memory and calls for our acknowledgment. Finally, it marks renewal: what was "formerly" has been fulfilled in Christ, inviting the reader to place themselves not in the past, but in the newness of the promise.

sens: That has existed for a long time, belonging to the past
Worn out by time or use
That is outdated, replaced by something new
The old nature or condition before transformation in Christ
G3820.detail:
1. That has existed for a long time, belonging to the past: this is the simplest meaning, that of what is ancient. For example, an old covenant (2 Corinthians 3:14 refers to the "old covenant"), or an old commandment (1 John 2:7 speaks of "an old commandment").
2. Worn out by time or use, tired and damaged: the word describes things that deteriorate. An old garment tears easily (Matthew 9:16: "a piece of new cloth on an old garment"), or an old wineskin bursts under the pressure of new wine (Mark 2:22).
3. That is outdated, replaced by something new, and must be abandoned: this is a contrast with what is new or fresh. Old leaven must be removed before the Passover (1 Corinthians 5:8: "not with old leaven").
4. The old nature or condition before transformation in Christ: the word spiritually describes what we had before our conversion. Romans 6:6 speaks of the "old man" crucified with Christ, that is, our past life under sin.
G3820.origine: The Greek word comes from the primary meaning of the verb that means "to be old or past." It stands in opposition to "new" (Greek: νέος or καινός). In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "yašèn" (that which has aged) or "bāleh" (that which wears out). The family of the word includes temporal meanings: that which dates from before, that which has lasted a long time.
G3820.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament. It is first used in the literal sense for objects: worn-out clothes (Matthew 9:16-17), tired wineskins (Mark 2:21-22, Luke 5:36-37). It also describes theological realities: the old covenant (2 Corinthians 3:14), an old commandment (1 John 2:7), the old leaven of malice to be removed (1 Corinthians 5:7-8). The most important spiritual meaning is found in Romans 6:6, Ephesians 4:22, and Colossians 3:9: the "old man" or the "old nature" in contrast with the new man created in Christ. In each context, the term carries the idea that the old must disappear to make way for the new.
G3820.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand that in Christ, he is no longer bound to his old life of sin. The "old man" has been crucified, which concretely means that we are freed from the bondage of sin. The image of new wine tearing old wineskins also reminds us that the new life does not accommodate our old habits: we are called to put off our past behaviors to put on the new man. It is a call to radical and ongoing transformation in our walk with Christ.

sens: that which is old, worn out by time
the outdated nature of something
obsolescence
the break with an old order
G3821.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is ancient, what has aged. It refers to the idea of something that has lost its vigor with the passage of time, like an old letter whose ink fades (Romans 7:6).
2. More specifically, antiquity evokes the outdated, surpassed nature of a provision. The "letter that has aged" (γράμματος, the letter of the Law) no longer has the binding force it once had, because the believer has died to the law.
3. The word thus expresses a break: the Christian no longer lives under the old regime of legal obligation, but in the newness of the Spirit. Antiquity characterizes the regime before Christ, in contrast with the newness of salvation in Him.
G3821.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective παλαιός (old, ancient), which first expresses advanced age, then obsolescence. This root goes back to the fundamental idea of time passing and wearing things out. In Romans 7:6, the antiquity of the letter stands in contrast to the newness of the Spirit, poles of Paul's theology of the change of era.
G3821.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 7:6. Paul uses it in the context of his explanation about the relationship between the Law and grace. Antiquity is that of the letter, the legal system based on external obedience to written commandments. It expresses not a moral judgment (the Law is not bad), but the observation that the old regime, based on the flesh and the letter, has given way to the new regime of the Spirit. It is a theological antiquity: the transition from the Old Testament to the New Testament, from bondage to freedom.
G3821.portee: This word helps the believer understand that he no longer lives under the influence of guilt and legal condemnation. Christ has freed the believer from the antiquity of the Mosaic regime to place him in the newness of life according to the Spirit. It is a word of freedom and transformation: the Christian life is not an accumulation of efforts to satisfy an old letter, but a walk guided by the living Spirit.

sens: To become worn out and deteriorated by time and use
To weaken and decline towards the end
To render old, to declare obsolete
G3822.detail:
1. To age is primarily the physical process by which something wears out and deteriorates due to the passage of time. It is like a garment that is worn for a long time: it becomes fragile, loses its colors, and eventually falls apart. The Bible uses it for fabrics and material goods that wear out (Luke 12:33 speaks of a purse that "wears out").
2. To age also denotes the natural decline towards disappearance or the end. A garment ages until it can no longer be used, as shown in the Psalms: clothes become unusable. Hebrews 1:11 compares heaven and earth to garments that "will age" and disappear.
3. In a broader and figurative sense, to age can mean to declare something old or obsolete, thus rendering it worthless. Hebrews 8:13 uses this word to say that God has "declared" the first covenant old by announcing a new covenant: it is now surpassed and "aged," that is, on the verge of disappearing.
G3822.origine: The word comes from the adjective "old" (παλαιός). It designates the process that makes something old — that causes it to age. In Hebrew, it generally corresponds to the verb "to wear out" (בלה). It shares the same root in the idea of wear and the passage of time: what is old has undergone the destructive action of the years.
G3822.emploi: This verb appears three times in the New Testament, always to describe an irreversible decline. In Luke 12:33, it refers to a fabric purse that wears out through natural use. In Hebrews 1:11, it describes the heavens and the earth at the end of time, having aged like a torn garment. In Hebrews 8:13, it takes on a theological significance: the first covenant is declared "aged" by the arrival of the new covenant in Jesus. The word thus shifts from the physical and natural to the spiritual and theological.
G3822.portee: This word reminds the reader that everything temporal — our possessions, our bodies, the structures of this world — is destined to age and disappear. But for the believer, it is an invitation: since material goods wear out, one must place their treasure elsewhere (Luke 12:33). More profoundly, the image of the aging of the old covenant and of heaven shows that God fulfills His promises and renews His relationship with humanity in Jesus Christ.

sens: Sporting contest where two opponents grapple with each other
Violent effort to overcome an opponent or to overcome a difficulty
Spiritual battle of the Christian against the powers of evil
G3823.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a sporting contest where two wrestlers face each other in a physical struggle — a very vivid image for Greek and Roman readers who were well acquainted with this sport. This is the primary meaning of the word.

2. By extension, the term applies to any intense struggle or conflict: a fierce effort to overcome any resistance or opposition.

3. Spiritually, Paul uses it in Ephesians 6:12 to describe the Christian's battle: not against visible enemies ("flesh and blood"), but against principalities and wicked spirits. The Christian's struggle is real, intense, physical — Paul chooses this precise word to show that it is not an abstraction.
G3823.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to shake" or "to agitate": the starting image is the violent movement of the body in wrestling. It belongs to a family of words expressing intense physical effort. It is a common Greek word in the sporting context of the Mediterranean world.
G3823.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 6:12. Paul uses it to characterize the spiritual battle of the believer: it is not an abstract or purely internal struggle, but a serious reality, requiring strength and vigilance, comparable to a real physical fight. The context shows that the Christian's struggle targets the invisible powers that govern darkness.
G3823.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian faith does not dwell in passive tranquility. The Christian is engaged in a real struggle against evil — as real as a physical fight. Paul uses the image of struggle to say: it is serious, it is demanding, it is a true trial. But it should be noted that a struggle is also a meeting where one can grow and overcome.

sens: Spiritual renewal of a person through baptism and the action of the Holy Spirit
Future and complete restoration of all things at the end of time
G3824.detail:
1. Regeneration primarily refers to the spiritual transformation of a person: it is a new birth, a new birth to divine life. In Titus 3:5, Paul links it to baptism and the Holy Spirit, which brings salvation not by our efforts, but by God's mercy. This is the heart of Christian conversion.

2. The word also applies to the complete restoration of the universe at the final judgment. In Matthew 19:28, Jesus speaks of the "renewal of all things" — the moment when the Son of Man will return in His glory and everything will be renewed. This is eschatological hope: not only are believers regenerated now, but the entire world will be at the last day.
G3824.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek "palin" (again) and "genesis" (birth, origin). It literally means "new birth" or "new creation." Stoics and Jewish apocalyptic writers used this term to speak of cosmic restoration. The word is found only in these two verses in the New Testament.
G3824.emploi: The word "regeneration" appears twice in the New Testament. In Titus 3:5, Paul uses it to refer to the inner renewal of the believer — the moment when God saves us through baptism and the Spirit. In Matthew 19:28, Jesus uses it to speak of the final and universal restoration of all things, when He will sit on His throne of glory. These two uses show that regeneration operates on two levels: personal and cosmic, now and at the end of time.
G3824.portee: This word enriches the Christian faith in two ways. First, it assures us that our conversion is not our work, but God's — a true new birth, free and merciful. Secondly, it opens hope: the world is not destined for eternal destruction, but for renewal. Our personal regeneration is an anticipated participation in the regeneration of the entire universe.

sens: once more, anew, at a later time
in return, again in the opposite direction
moreover, additionally, in a statement that adds a new element
on the other hand, in contrast to what precedes
G3825.detail:
1. The most common meaning: an action repeats or reproduces itself after having occurred once. Example: "Jesus began to teach again by the sea" (Mark 4:1) — He resumes His teaching as He has done before.
2. The word indicates a movement of return, a back-and-forth: the action returns to its starting point or reverses direction. Example: "And the disciples returned home" (John 20:10) — they go back to their house.
3. In discourse, "again" means "moreover" or "additionally": a new statement or argument is added that extends what has been said. Example: "What then do you want me to do?" (Mark 15:12) — Pilate resumes speaking to continue the debate.
4. By contrast or in counterpart: the word can introduce an opposing or complementary viewpoint. Example: "Luke 6:43" — a good tree bears good fruit, and conversely, a bad tree bears bad fruit.
G3825.origine: The Greek word παλιν (palin) fundamentally expresses the idea of repetition or return. It comes from a root meaning "to turn" or "to go back." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word שׁוּב (shouv), which means "to turn," "to return," or "to repent." This relationship shows that the word carries the image of movement that restarts, whether in time (again) or in space (returning to a place).
G3825.emploi: The word "again" appears about 140 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew and John, who frequently use it to recount a succession of events or words. In Matthew, it often describes Jesus' repeated actions: He teaches "again," He speaks "again to the devil." In John, it highlights key moments: Jesus asks Peter "do you love me?" "again" (John 21:16). In rhetoric, "again" can also introduce a complementary argument ("moreover") or a contrast ("on the other hand"). The word has no moral nuance: it simply states that an action or word repeats or returns.
G3825.portee: This ordinary word reveals how the Bible presents the actions of God and men: not as isolated acts, but as movements that repeat, that engage in dialogue with what comes before. For the reader, this emphasizes the importance of waiting and returning: Jesus will return, we have multiple opportunities to believe or refuse, and God's grace acts continually. The word also invites us to recognize the patterns of sacred history: the same lessons return because the human heart needs to hear, again and again.

sens: All at once, in one voice
En masse, without distinction
Collectively, as a whole
G3826.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of several people acting or speaking at the same moment, in one voice, without letting the other speak. In Luke 23:18, the crowd cries "together": "Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas"—all the cries blend into a single tumult, with no one listening.
2. It also conveys the idea of a compact mass, where individuals disappear behind the group, where no one stands out. The crowd here acts as a block, swept along by the collective movement, each reinforcing the voice of the other.
3. The word emphasizes the absence of division: no one objects, no one steps out of line, all agree in the same way, as if a single thought animates them.
G3826.origine: The word comes from two roots: "pan" or "pas" which means "all, each," and "plèthos" which means "multitude, crowd." By joining them, we get the image of the whole together, of the totality acting in unison. It is a rare adverb in classical Greek, but it aptly conveys the unanimity of a crowd.
G3826.emploi: This word appears only once in the Gospels: in Luke 23:18, at the moment of Jesus' trial before Pilate. The gathered crowd cries together to demand Jesus' death and the release of Barabbas. This unique usage was sufficient for the evangelist to depict the power of popular tumult, where each individual voice dissolves into the collective roar.
G3826.portee: This word shows us how a crowd can push individuals in unison toward injustice, each amplifying the voices of others. It serves as a biblical warning about the power of collective pressure and the difficulty for a single voice to oppose a raging multitude.

sens: Coastal region of ancient Asia Minor
G3828.detail: 1. Pamphylia is a province in southern Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), located between Cilicia to the east and Lycia to the southeast. It appears in the account of Paul's missionary journeys: the ship that carried him to Rome sailed along its coasts (Acts 27:5), and Paul preached there while passing through the city of Perge (Acts 13:13). It is a region that the early Christians traversed while proclaiming the Gospel.
G3828.origine: The Greek name Pamphylia literally means "land of all peoples," from the Greek pan (all) and phulé (people, tribe). It is a historically well-known region of the Mediterranean antiquity, with its important ports.
G3828.emploi: Pamphylia is mentioned five times in Acts, always in connection with the journeys of Paul and Barnabas. It first appears at Pentecost when Peter enumerates the regions from which the faithful witnesses of the Holy Spirit's gift came (Acts 2:10). Then, Paul and Barnabas land there during their first missionary journey at Perge (Acts 13:13), where John Mark abandons them and returns to Jerusalem—this later becomes a point of disagreement between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:38). They pass through it again on their return (Acts 14:24), and Paul's ship sails along it on the way to Rome (Acts 27:5). These mentions show that Pamphylia was a strategic passage point for the expansion of early Christianity toward the East.
G3828.portee: Pamphylia reminds us that the Gospel spread through concrete regions of the Mediterranean world, not magically but through the travel, preaching, and trials of the apostles. It also illustrates the reality of human failures (John Mark abandoning Paul) at the heart of the success of divine mission.

sens: Establishment that welcomes travelers and their pack animals
Place of lodging and refuge for passing strangers
G3829.detail:
1. An inn is a building intended to accommodate travelers and their mounts. It is a public place where one receives those arriving from afar. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the Samaritan "put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him" (Luke 10:34): he entrusts the wounded man to the innkeeper for care and lodging.
2. By extension, the inn symbolizes a refuge, a place of comfort and care. It welcomes those in need, the stranger, the vulnerable traveler. It is here that mercy is expressed: by bringing the wounded man to the inn, the Samaritan does not settle for first aid; he offers him true rest and genuine protection.
G3829.origine: The Greek word pandocheion comes from a root meaning "to welcome everyone" (pan = all, and dokhé = welcome). It is a late word, an evolved form of classical Greek. It literally designates a caravanserai, an Eastern roadside inn, a place where caravans would stop. The Greek word reflects the Palestinian context: these inns are the khans of the Middle Eastern roads, essential for travelers.
G3829.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 10:34, in the famous parable of the Good Samaritan. This teaching story, which asks who is my neighbor, features a wounded man left on the road. The priest and the Levite pass by without acting; only the Samaritan, despised by the Jews, has compassion. He bandages the wounds of the injured man with oil and wine, places him on his animal, brings him to the inn, and pays the innkeeper to care for him. The inn here is an extension of compassion: it is not just lodging; it is a haven of healing.
G3829.portee: This word speaks to us about Christian hospitality and care for the weak. The inn in the parable of the Samaritan is not just a backdrop: it embodies practical and lasting help, the refusal to abandon the suffering. For the Christian, it is a call not to pass indifferently before misery, but to offer refuge, care, and protection to those in need, without restriction of clan or favoritism.

sens: one who runs an inn or guesthouse
one who welcomes travelers and provides lodging for a fee
G3830.detail:
1. The innkeeper is the owner or manager of an inn, that is, an establishment where travelers can stay and eat. In the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:35), Jesus shows the Samaritan entrusting the wounded man to the innkeeper with money to take care of him.
2. By extension, it is one who practices the profession of welcoming travelers: he receives them, lodges them, feeds them, and depends on his income to live. The word evokes availability and service rendered to passing strangers.
G3830.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "pan-" (all) and "dokeus" (one who receives). The idea is one who receives everyone, who opens up to all travelers. It is a late form of Attic Greek "pandokeus." The word designates a well-established profession in the Greco-Roman world, where trade routes and pilgrimages made inns indispensable.
G3830.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:35. Jesus places it in the parable of the Good Samaritan to illustrate practical mercy. The innkeeper represents one who can continue the work of aid begun: he is capable of caring for the wounded man and providing him with lodging and food. His role shows that charity can also be exercised through intermediaries and that those who have the means should put them at the service of others.
G3830.portee: The mention of the innkeeper in this parable teaches us that love for one's neighbor is not limited to direct gestures. It also invites us to recognize and support those who, in their professions, have the capacity to welcome and serve. It is a call to the responsibility of each towards those who suffer, and to trust those who help us in the work of mercy.

sens: Group of all members of a household, from the head to the youngest child, including servants
G3832.detail: 1. The word paints a scene of domestic life: the entire household gathered together. In Acts 16:34, after his conversion, the jailer of Philippi welcomes Paul and Silas "with all his family" — that is, all those who live in his house, from the oldest to the youngest. It is an image of joy shared by everyone, a communion under the same roof.
G3832.origine: The word comes from two roots: "pan" (all, each) and "oikos" (house, family). It is a late Greek formation, never perfectly regular in classical Greek. It translates Hebrew phrases where "house" means all the inhabitants (as in Exodus 1:1, "all the house of Israel"). The adverb emphasizes totality: no one is excluded from the scene.
G3832.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 16:34). It is a pivotal moment: the jailer becomes a believer because of the apostle Paul, and his conversion is not solitary or secret — it becomes an occasion for a family celebration where everyone in his house rejoices in the new faith. The Bible thus emphasizes that grace transforms not only an individual but an entire household.
G3832.portee: This passage reminds us that faith does not confine one to spiritual solitude: it creates communion, it brings loved ones together. When a heart converts, those who love and live under its roof can receive the blessing. It is an encouragement for the believer: their faith can be a light for their entire household.

sens: Warrior equipment covering the entire body of the warrior
Complete set of spiritual weapons and defenses for the fight against evil
G3833.detail:
1. The full armor is the war equipment that protects the entire body of the soldier: helmet, breastplate, shield, sword. It is the image of a well-equipped warrior preparing for battle (Luke 11:22 speaks of one who removes all the weapons from a defeated opponent).
2. Figuratively, God's armor refers to the entire set of spiritual means that God gives to the Christian to resist evil and the action of the devil. Just as a soldier must don his complete equipment to face the enemy, the believer must put on all of God's weapons — that is, truth, righteousness, faith, salvation, the word of God — to stand firm in spiritual battle (Ephesians 6:11, 6:13).
G3833.origine: The Greek word panoplia comes from two words: pas (all) and hoplon (weapon, shield). It literally refers to the complete equipment of the Greek hoplite warrior, each piece being essential for overall protection. In Hebrew, the word חֲלִיצָה (halitsa) can refer to the spoils or the entire equipment. The military image of armor has naturally served as a metaphor in biblical text to express spiritual protection.
G3833.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in contexts of combat. In Luke 11:22, Jesus speaks of one who removes the full armor from a defeated warrior — an image of the triumph of the stronger. But it is especially in Ephesians 6:11 and 6:13 that the word takes on its full spiritual significance: Paul exhorts Christians to put on all of God's weapons to resist the schemes of the devil and stand firm in the evil day. The emphasis on "all the weapons" underscores that protection must be total and complete, not fragmented.
G3833.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the life of faith is not a passive life but an active engagement against evil. God's armor is not a poetic fantasy: it refers to the concrete resources that God offers — His truth, His righteousness, His word — so that we are not overcome by temptations and trials. It is a call to equip ourselves completely, without negligence, strengthening our dependence on God rather than relying on our own strength.

sens: Malicious skill, habit of deceiving by indirect means
Hidden calculation or strategy to deceive someone
Subtle deception, particularly in speech or teaching
G3834.detail: 1. Cunning is a form of active malice — not just a simple clumsy deception, but a perverted intelligence that unfolds to deceive. When the Pharisees try to trap Jesus with a question about the denarius, Jesus sees their cunning (Luke 20:23): they use a question that seems innocent but is actually aimed at compromising Him. 2. It is also the calculation that hides behind appearances. The wisdom of the world that takes the wise in their cunning (1 Corinthians 3:19) shows that cunning characterizes reasoning closed to the truth of God — a too-clever calculation that ensnares itself in its own trap. 3. In the context of preaching and teaching, cunning refers to the manipulation of the word: Paul refuses to have a cunning conduct or to distort the word of God (2 Corinthians 4:2), meaning twisting the message to serve hidden interests. Even the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning (2 Corinthians 11:3) — a subtle corruption of thoughts. 4. Finally, cunning can become a systematic method of leading astray: it is employed in the seductive means of false teachers who want to divert us from simplicity toward Christ (Ephesians 4:14).
G3834.origine: The Greek word panourgia comes from pan ("all") and ergon ("work", "action"), the initial idea being a skill that operates everywhere, a versatility. In classical Greek, this word oscillated between admiration for intelligent cunning and moral condemnation of deception. In the Bible, particularly in Greek (translation of the Hebrew armah), it almost always designates malicious cunning — an intelligence put to the service of lies or deception.
G3834.emploi: The word panourgia appears five times in the New Testament, all usages belonging to Paul or the account of Luke. Luke uses it once to describe the calculation of Jesus' adversaries (Luke 20:23). Paul uses it four times to stigmatize a form of worldly wisdom that opposes the simplicity of the Gospel: he denounces the cunning of human wisdom (1 Corinthians 3:19), personally refuses to resort to it in his ministry (2 Corinthians 4:2), recalls the danger that the subtlety of the tempter presents for the purity of faith (2 Corinthians 11:3), and warns against the cunning of false teachers who lead astray the churches (Ephesians 4:14). The word always carries a negative connotation: it characterizes the opposite of uprightness.
G3834.portee: Cunning reminds us that lies can be refined, intelligent, seductive — particularly when they wrap around the word of God or Christian doctrine. It is a call to vigilance: remaining simple toward Christ means rejecting not only gross lies but also subtle calculations, manipulations of the truth, twisted doctrines. The Spirit keeps us from cunning by giving us transparency in faith.

sens: Skill in deceiving, using indirect means to obtain what one wants
Sagacity, prudence in action
G3835.detail:
1. Cunning is the art of deceiving someone through skillful and indirect means. It is the ability to act with finesse to achieve one's goal without the other seeing it coming. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 12:16 when he says, "as a crafty man, I caught you by cunning": he acknowledges having acted with a certain calculated malice towards the Corinthians, for example, by not directly asking them for money but approaching it differently.
2. The word can also denote positive sagacity: the prudent and intelligent skill to navigate difficult situations. This nuance is more apparent in the passages where he describes the wisdom of the humble in the face of the powerful.
G3835.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and originally designates one who is "ready for anything" (pan = all, ourgos = work, action). It combines the idea of limitless activity with that of malice. In the Septuagint, it translates the Hebrew "arum" (עָרוּם), which means naked or devoid, then by extension cunning, one who sheds naivety. The word often has a negative connotation in classical Greek.
G3835.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:16. Paul uses it ironically to acknowledge that he, an apostle, acted towards the Corinthians with a certain cunning — perhaps by deliberately refusing their money in a calculated way, which somewhat "trapped" them despite himself. It is a rhetorical concession: Paul accepts the charge of cunning to show the absurdity of the accusations against him. The context indicates that Paul is defending his integrity, and this word serves to expose his adversaries through irony rather than boast of dishonesty.
G3835.portee: This passage invites reflection on apostolic authenticity and the tension between sagacity and righteousness. Even Paul, in defending himself, acknowledges that God's servants can use cunning — but always in the service of truth, never to deceive or exploit. It is a call to examine our own motives: are we cunning to serve the Gospel or to serve ourselves?

sens: In all places, without exception
In all cases, under all circumstances
Universally or generally
G3837.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: everywhere denotes all places without exception. When the Gospel says that Jesus' fame "spread everywhere" (Mark 1:28), it means it spread throughout all regions, in all nearby villages. After the resurrection, the disciples "went out to preach everywhere" (Mark 16:20), meaning in all places where they could announce the Good News.
2. The word is also used to express completeness in time or circumstances: at all times, in all situations. When God announces "in all places" that people should repent (Acts 17:30), it means this call applies to everyone, everywhere men are found. Similarly, to acknowledge something "everywhere with gratitude" (Acts 24:3) means to acknowledge it uniformly, without exception.
G3837.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and is formed from the root "pan" (all) and "tachos" (spatial arrangement, position). It expresses the idea of "in all places." It is a simple and direct adverb: no nuance, no restriction — everywhere truly means everywhere. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words that also express the totality of space.
G3837.emploi: This word appears seven times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and the Gospels. It first describes the spread of the Good News and the ministry of Jesus (Mark 1:28, Luke 9:6, Mark 16:20): the apostles are sent to preach everywhere, healings happen everywhere. Then, it expresses the universality of the divine call (Acts 17:30: God announces repentance to all men in all places) or the extension of a reality (Acts 28:22: the Christian sect encounters opposition everywhere). Each usage emphasizes that the action or reality being discussed is not limited to a single place or case.
G3837.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the Gospel is intended for all places and all people: there is no place on earth where God is not at work or where His call to repentance does not apply. It also emphasizes that the early Church never settled for a single location but carried the Good News wherever it could go. It is a call to the universality of the Christian mission.

sens: In a total manner, without exception or reservation
Entirely, from beginning to end
Definitively, without possibility of return
G3838.detail:
1. Completely means without any limit or restriction. In Luke 13:11, the bent woman "could not stand up at all": she could in no way regain her upright posture, her infirmity was total.
2. The word also describes an action carried out to its final and complete end. In Hebrews 7:25, Christ is able to save "perfectly" those who draw near to God: He saves them in a complete, definitive way, lacking nothing in their salvation.
3. The underlying idea is that of flawless accomplishment — nothing is spared, nothing is left aside.
G3838.origine: The word comes from two roots: "pan" (all) and "telos" (end, completion). It thus designates what goes all the way, what is brought to its complete end. It is the idea of the whole reaching its term, of the complete that omits nothing.
G3838.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 13:11, it describes the total physical incapacity of the possessed woman. In Hebrews 7:25, it characterizes the power of Christ: He saves completely and definitively, always ready to intercede. Both contexts emphasize a flawless totality — whether it is a total bodily failure or an unlimited capacity for salvation.
G3838.portee: This word invites us to grasp the magnitude of what Christ accomplishes for us. His salvation is not partial or provisional: He saves us entirely, once for all. This is a fundamental assurance for anyone who approaches God through Christ.

sens: From all sides
In all respects
Entirely, without exception
G3839.detail:
1. "From all sides" or "everywhere": the word denotes what extends in all directions or to all places. In Acts 24:3, Paul speaks of gratitude towards Felix "in all and everywhere" — he means: in all aspects, in every regard, on every occasion.
2. "In all respects" or "in every way": it is the idea that something is valid, applies, or must be understood without restriction, from a global perspective. Here, Paul's gratitude towards Felix is expressed completely, without reservation.
3. "Entirely, without exception": the adverb marks totality or the absence of limit. Paul does not thank Felix partially, but "totally" — fully and without shadow.
G3839.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "pas" (πᾶς), which means "all." This very common adjective in Greek serves to form several adverbs: "pantē" is a variant that emphasizes the global or total manner of an action. It is a typical Greek way of saying "everywhere and completely."
G3839.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 24:3, in the speech of Tertullus (a lawyer speaking on behalf of the Jewish authorities before the Roman governor Felix). Tertullus expresses gratitude towards Felix "in all and everywhere" — that is, in all respects, in every way. The adverb reinforces the idea of total and unreserved acknowledgment. It is an oratorical, solemn usage, typical of the formal style of Roman pleadings.
G3839.portee: This word reminds us that authentic gratitude towards one who acts well is not measured or partial: it encompasses all good actions and is expressed straightforwardly. For the believer, this invites us to recognize with generosity and totality the blessings received from God and others, without restriction or ulterior motives.

sens: From every direction, without exception
Which completely envelops, surrounds
G3840.detail:
1. The word describes a presence or action that comes from all sides at once, leaving no escape. In Mark 1:45, crowds come to Jesus "from all sides" because the news of his miracles has spread everywhere: he can no longer enter a town without being immediately surrounded. In Luke 19:43, the enemies of Jerusalem will encircle him "from all sides" with trenches, meaning in such a way as to block every access. The idea is one of an unbroken totality.
2. Sometimes the word describes rather what covers, completely envelops. In Hebrews 9:4, the ark of the covenant was "covered" with gold on all sides, entirely covered, with no part left uncovered.
G3840.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "pais" (all) to which the suffix "-then" is added, indicating the origin or direction "from where." It literally means "from where all," that is, "from everywhere." It is already found in the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), notably in Jeremiah to translate the Hebrew "kol" (all).
G3840.emploi: This word appears three times in the New Testament, always to evoke a spatial totality.
