In the first two passages (Mark and Luke), it describes the movement of people or enemies converging towards a central point: the crowds flocking to Jesus from everywhere, or the enemy troops surrounding the city from all sides. In the third passage (Hebrews 9:4), the context is different: it is not about movement, but about the complete covering of an object — the gold that covers the ark on all sides. The adverb thus maintains a coherence: it always expresses the idea of a totality without exception.
G3840.portee: This word reminds us how the presence of Jesus or his action spreads irresistibly, touching people "from all sides." It also shows how judgment can encircle a city or a people, leaving no way out. For the believer, it is an image of totality — whether it is the complete covering of the sanctuary by gold (a sign of his absolute holiness) or the universal radiance of the Good News.

sens: He who possesses all authority and all power
He whose power extends over all things
God in his sovereign majesty
G3841.detail:
1. The word designates one who holds supreme power, absolute authority over the entire universe. In Revelation 1:8, Jesus himself is called "the Almighty," affirming that he is "the one who is, who was, and who is to come": this means that he dominates the past, present, and future. It is a power that operates without limits.

2. This title emphasizes that God has unrestrained strength, capable of accomplishing his purposes despite any opposition. In Revelation 11:17, the elders thank the Lord God for having "taken his great power and begun to reign": this is not a theoretical power, but a concrete action that subjects all creation to the divine plan.

3. The term also evokes the majesty and holiness of God. In Revelation 4:8, the heavenly creatures sing: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty" — his power is inseparable from his absolute moral perfection.
G3841.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: *pas* (all) and *kratos* (strength, power, dominion). The image is that of a hand that holds or masters everything. In the Greek Old Testament, this title primarily translates the Hebrew name Shadday (שַׁדַּי), the "Mighty God" or the one who "is sufficient," and also the expression "God of hosts" (צָבָא). It is a very ancient title, already used in the Psalms and the Prophets to exalt the sovereign power of God.
G3841.emploi: The word appears only 10 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Revelation and once in 2 Corinthians. In 2 Corinthians 6:18, Paul cites a divine promise and calls God "Lord Almighty" to guarantee his commitment to the believers — his power makes this promise of being a father to them inviolable. In Revelation, the title becomes recurrent: it asserts that despite chaos and persecution, God and the Lamb maintain absolute authority over history. In Revelation 16:7, the saints acknowledge that God's judgments are "true and just" because they proceed from the one who holds all power. The revealing context emphasizes that this power is not brute, but linked to justice and the final victory of Good.
G3841.portee: This title reminds the Christian that God is never overwhelmed, never defeated, and that his promises hold because they rest on limitless power. In the face of challenges, persecutions, or doubts, confessing God as Almighty is an act of faith that affirms: my Father truly controls everything, even what seems out of control to me. It is a power always directed towards good and justice, not towards arbitrariness.

sens: at all times, without interruption
on every occasion, regularly
constantly, without exception
in a habitual or customary manner
G3842.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of continuous and uninterrupted time: an action or situation that persists without ceasing. Jesus tells the disciples that they will have "always" the poor with them (Matthew 26:11), meaning that this reality will never cease. Likewise, the Father never leaves Jesus alone; He is "always" with him (John 8:29).
2. The word also designates a repetition every time, on every occasion: to do something "always" means to do it regularly, without fail. Paul gives thanks to God "continually" for the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 1:2), meaning every time he prays, without exception.
3. It also expresses constancy and absence of variation: a quality that remains the same under all circumstances. Jesus does "always" what pleases his Father (John 8:29), for his obedience never varies.
4. Finally, it emphasizes habit or a lasting disposition: a characteristic and persevering way of being. Paul exhorts believers to rejoice "always" (Philippians 4:4) and to give thanks "always" for all things (Ephesians 5:20), as a permanent attitude of their life in Christ.
G3842.origine: The word comes from the Greek "pâs" (πᾶς), which means "all" or "each." The adverb "pantote" combines the idea of all (pàs) with that of time, hence its meaning of "at all times" or "in every circumstance." It is a late word, used mainly from the New Testament, where it frequently appears in the writings of the Apostle Paul to express the idea of permanence or constancy.
G3842.emploi: The word appears 37 times in the New Testament, very often in the Pauline epistles. It is used in various contexts: to describe perseverance in prayer and thanksgiving (1 Thessalonians 1:2, 2 Thessalonians 1:3), obedience to God (John 8:29), divine presence (John 8:29, Hebrews 7:25), or the exhortation to constancy in moral and spiritual life (1 Thessalonians 5:16, Philippians 4:4). The Gospels use it to evoke permanent truths ("you will always have the poor," Matthew 26:11). In Paul, it often emphasizes the continuity of his prayer, his thanksgiving, or his apostolic commitment, marking the permanent orientation of his life towards God and the churches.
G3842.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of perseverance and constancy in spiritual life. It invites an attitude of continuous prayer, of thanksgiving that is constantly renewed, and of faithful obedience, not as a heroic effort at a single moment, but as the lasting orientation of life in Christ. It also teaches that God himself is "always" present and faithful, which should strengthen the believer's trust in all circumstances.

sens: without any doubt, certainly
by all means, absolutely
in a complete negation: not at all
in a partial negation: not absolutely
G3843.detail:
1. Without any doubt, certainly: this is to affirm something with strength and assurance. In Acts 28:4, the barbarians see Paul bitten by a snake and think: "Certainly this man is a murderer" — they are convinced, without hesitation. This is also the meaning in Luke 4:23, where Jesus says that people will undoubtedly apply a well-known saying to him.
2. By all means, absolutely: this expresses a strong and irrevocable intention. In Acts 18:21, Paul declares that he must "absolutely" celebrate the next feast in Jerusalem — it is a firm decision.
3. In a complete negation: not at all, in no way. In Romans 3:9, Paul asks if the Jews are "better" than the Greeks, and answers: "Not at all" — it is a total refusal.
4. In a partial negation: not entirely, not absolutely. In 1 Corinthians 5:10, Paul says that one should not separate "absolutely" from the immoral of the world — it is a restriction of the previous command.
G3843.origine: This word comes from the Greek "pas" (all) and expresses the idea of totality, completeness. It appears in the Greek Old Testament in a few passages (like the translation of 2 Kings 5:11). The word belongs to the family of adverbs that modify the intensity of an affirmation or negation: it reinforces what precedes it by marking it as total and unreserved.
G3843.emploi: "Pantôs" appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in Acts. Without negation, it expresses assurance in an affirmation (Luke 4:23, Acts 28:4), or a firm, irrevocable will (Acts 18:21, 1 Corinthians 9:10, 9:22, 16:12). With a negation, it nuances the refusal: either it makes it absolute (Romans 3:9: not at all), or it limits it (1 Corinthians 5:10: not absolutely). The adverb thus changes its role according to its context: it reinforces or moderates depending on what surrounds it.
G3843.portee: This word teaches us the strength of conviction and assurance in Christ. When Paul or Jesus uses it to affirm something, it is with unreserved certainty. It also shows us the important nuance in obedience: sometimes Scripture rejects a behavior "absolutely" (like sin), sometimes it only refuses the "absolute" excess (like total separation from the world). Learning to distinguish these two uses helps us to read God's will correctly.

sens: Next to, close to (in space)
At someone's home, in the house or dwelling of
From, coming from (source or origin)
By, from (indicating the agent in passive)
According to, in front of, in the eyes of (comparison or judgment)
Against, contrary to (opposition or violation)
G3844.detail:
1. The word describes a spatial position: to be or to place oneself next to something or someone. Example: the disciples of Jesus are sitting "near" him by the sea (Mark 4:1).
2. It is used to say that one lives, stays, or dwells with someone. Example: when Jesus asks for hospitality, he is received "near" someone (John 1:39; Luke 11:37).
3. It indicates the source or origin of something: it is from that side that the word, action, news comes. Example: Jesus says he comes "from" the Father (John 1:14); one asks "from" someone for alms (Acts 3:2).
4. After a verb in the passive, it names the one who performs the action, like "by" in French. Example: the Pharisees "sent by" the chief priests arrive (Mark 14:43).
5. It measures or compares by saying in front of whom, according to what one judges: what is worth much "in front of" God is not always what impresses men (Romans 2:13).
6. It expresses opposition or violation: to act "against" the law, or "in violation" of a received instruction (2 Thessalonians 3:6).
G3844.origine: This word comes from a Greek root meaning "next to" or "near." It is a very rich preposition, which combines with three different cases of the noun (genitive, dative, accusative) and takes on nuances depending on the context. In composition, it enters into compound verbs like "παραλαμβάνω" (to receive, to take to oneself) or "παράγω" (to pass by). In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, it often renders Hebrew prepositions like מִן (from) or אֵצֶל (near).
G3844.emploi: This preposition appears 184 times in the New Testament. It is extremely frequent in the four Gospels, especially to situate Jesus and his disciples: near the sea, in houses, with the sick. It is also used to indicate the one from whom an action comes (to ask something "from" someone, to receive "from" someone), and particularly to name the agent after a verb in the passive. In Paul, it often takes on a metaphorical or ethical sense: what is "in front of" God, what counts "in the eyes of" God. Its meaning varies according to the grammatical case of the following word and according to the context: spatial and physical in miracle narratives, more abstract and theological in the epistles.
G3844.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God and Jesus are not distant, but close, within reach. It emphasizes the idea of presence and relationship: being "near" someone signifies a form of intimacy or dependence. When we read that Jesus comes "from" the Father or that the disciples receive his words "from" him, it is to show the authenticity of the source. It is also a word that speaks from God's perspective: what has weight "in front of" God, what counts "in the eyes of" God invites the believer to align their heart with God's judgment rather than that of the world.

sens: To exceed a limit by crossing what separates
To violate a commandment, a law, a tradition
To abandon, to turn away from a responsibility or a promise
G3845.detail:
1. The word paints the image of someone who crosses a boundary or barrier (the preposition "para" means "beside, beyond"). It is to exceed what should not be exceeded, as when the disciples of Jesus "transgress the tradition of the elders" by not washing their hands before eating (Matthew 15:2): they have crossed the limit that tradition set.

2. The word mainly applies to the violation of a moral or religious rule. When one "transgresses the commandment of God" (Matthew 15:3), one has knowingly disobeyed what he has commanded: it is the act of pushing aside the law, of going beyond.

3. In a broader sense, "to transgress" also means "to abandon" a charge or a promise entrusted. Judas "abandoned" his apostleship (Acts 1:25), meaning he turned away from it to go elsewhere: the word emphasizes that he left the position that had been entrusted to him.
G3845.origine: The word comes from the Greek "para" (beside, beyond) and "bainô" (to walk, to go). The initial image is that of one who walks "beyond" the limit, who crosses what should not be crossed. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates Hebrew verbs meaning "to turn away" or "to go beyond" (like סוּר, "to turn away," or עָבַר, "to pass"), which shows that transgression is a voluntary deviation from a prescribed path.
G3845.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible: twice in Matthew (15:2 and 15:3), in the controversy between Jesus and the Pharisees about hand purity. The disciples "transgress" tradition by ignoring it, and the Pharisees "transgress" the commandment of God by preferring their own tradition. A third occurrence appears in Acts 1:25, where Judas has "abandoned" his ministry: here, the word emphasizes the rupture of an apostolic promise. In all cases, "to transgress" implies a conscious violation and a deviation from what was established.
G3845.portee: This word reminds readers that transgression is a voluntary crossing of a limit set by God or a legitimate authority. It also shows that what truly matters is obedience to the heart of God's command, not to human tradition that may contradict it. For the Christian, understanding transgression also means grasping the importance of keeping one's commitments and not turning away from them lightly.

sens: To navigate to a place by ship, setting a course in a direction
To arrive or land at a place after crossing
To progress at sea, moving forward by navigation
G3846.detail:
1. The verb means to navigate, to set sail towards a specific destination. The image is that of a ship heading towards a determined place while crossing the sea. In Acts 20:15, Paul and his companions "sailed towards Samos," meaning they set their course for that island with their boat.

2. More broadly, to sail refers to the action of arriving at a port or coastal place after a maritime crossing. It is the endpoint of the journey by boat.

3. The word can also simply evoke progression and advancement at sea, the act of navigating from one stage to another. The three verses in Acts 20:15 illustrate this continuous movement: from Chios to Samos, then to Miletus.
G3846.origine: The word is composed of "para" (towards, beside) and "ballō" (to throw, to cast). The basic idea is to throw oneself towards a place, to head there. In the maritime context, this original meaning has been specified to denote the action of sailing towards a destination. The Hebrew verb נָטָה (nâtâh, "to stretch, to incline") sometimes translates this notion of direction.
G3846.emploi: The verb "to sail" appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:15, during Paul's journey to Jerusalem after his stay in Asia. It is a technical term from maritime vocabulary. Paul and his companions progress from port to port: they sailed towards Samos after passing Chios. This context shows that the verb describes a deliberate and targeted movement of the ship towards a well-defined destination, step by step in the apostolic journey.
G3846.portee: This word reminds us of the concrete reality of the apostle Paul's travels to proclaim the Gospel. It shows us that the spread of the Good News was not through abstract routes, but through real, dangerous, and laborious maritime journeys. To sail towards a destination means to advance with determination and direction, which also illustrates Paul's determination to pursue his mission despite the perils.

sens: crossing an established limit
violation of a law or commandment
sin that consists of disobeying what has been commanded
act of guilt by which one exceeds a rule
G3847.detail:
1. Literally, the word evokes the idea of crossing a limit or exceeding a boundary that should not be crossed. It is the act of going beyond an established barrier: in Romans 4:15, the absence of law means there is no marked limit, thus no transgression possible.
2. Concretely, it is the violation of a specific law or commandment. When the Psalmist or the Apostle Paul speaks of transgression, he refers to an act by which one infringes what has been commanded. Romans 2:23 condemns one who teaches the law but transgresses it himself: he crosses the limit he proclaims.
3. Spiritually, it is sin viewed from the perspective of disobedience to a divine order. Unlike simple omission (the absence of good), transgression implies a conscious or unconscious will to cross what was forbidden. In 1 Timothy 2:14, Eve became guilty of transgression by crossing God's command.
4. The word emphasizes the inherent guilt of this act of exceeding: one can only transgress what exists and imposes itself. This is why Galatians 3:19 teaches that the law was given precisely because of transgressions, to clarify their seriousness and establish responsibility.
G3847.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb παραβαίνω (to cross, to exceed), formed from παρά (beyond, against) and βαίνω (to go, to walk). The image is that of someone who crosses a limit or a boundary that they should not exceed. In the Greek Old Testament, the word translates the Hebrew שֵׂט (deviation, deviation). The word family includes the verb "to transgress" and other derivatives evoking the exceeding or violation of an established rule.
G3847.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Paul's epistles and the epistle to the Hebrews. Paul uses it to theologize about the relationship between the law and sin: in Romans 4:15 and 5:14, he explains that transgression implies the existence of a law, and in Galatians 3:19, he asserts that the law was given precisely because of transgressions. In 1 Timothy 2:14, he applies it to Eve's fall. Hebrews 2:2 and 9:15 use it to speak of divine judgment against those who violate the revealed word. The meaning remains constant: a culpable crossing of a moral or legal limit established by God.
G3847.portee: Understanding that transgression is not a simple vague sin, but the conscious crossing of a limit that God has established and communicated. This helps the believer recognize that sin exists only where there is a law or commandment: this is why the revelation of divine will is so important. The word also reminds us that guilt arises when one knows what is commanded and yet exceeds it, which leads us to measure the grace of Christ who bears its consequences.

sens: one who crosses a limit
one who violates a law or commandment
one who disobeys God
G3848.detail:
1. Literally, one who crosses a limit or boundary — who goes over what was established. In Galatians 2:18, Paul speaks of one who rebuilds what he has destroyed, thus making himself a transgressor: this is crossing the limit of grace by returning to works.
2. One who violates a given law, particularly God's law. In Romans 2:25-27, Paul explains that if you transgress the law, your circumcision becomes worthless: you have crossed what the law commanded. In James 2:11, one who commits murder becomes a transgressor of the law, even if he does not commit adultery.
3. One who sins by violating God's commandments. In James 2:9, showing favoritism is committing a sin and being condemned by the law as a transgressor: it is actively disobeying what was commanded.
G3848.origine: The word comes from the verb meaning "to cross" or "to go beyond" (literally "to go beside" the limit). It designates one who has crossed an established barrier, who has gone over a rule. The root evokes the idea of exceeding, transgressing, violating a prohibition or law. In Hebrew, this word often translates terms meaning "one who rebels" or "one who transgresses."
G3848.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, all in Pauline epistles and in James. Paul uses it to show the absurdity of returning to the law after understanding its inability to save: one who transmits the law makes himself a transgressor (Galatians 2:18). In Romans 2:25-27, he uses it to demonstrate that circumcision is only beneficial if one keeps the law; otherwise, you are a transgressor. James uses it to remind that violating one commandment makes one a transgressor of the whole law (James 2:9, 2:11). The word emphasizes that sin is never small: it is always an active transgression of what God has established.
G3848.portee: This word reminds Christians that sin is not a passive weakness, but an active transgression — a voluntary crossing of the boundary that God has set. Understanding that we are transgressors brings us back to our need for grace and forgiveness. It also invites vigilance: returning on one's steps in faith risks making oneself a transgressor.

sens: To force someone to do something against their natural will
To constrain by physical force
To urgently implore, insistently urge someone to accept
G3849.detail: 1. The literal meaning of the word is to force something against its nature or law — it is a word that speaks of resistance overcome. However, in the New Testament, this theoretical meaning does not appear directly. 2. The second meaning, to constrain by physical force, also does not appear in the two biblical passages. 3. It is the third meaning that dominates: to press someone insistently, almost pleadingly, to get them to accept or do something. This is seen with Lydia in Acts 16:15, where she 'urged us with her insistence' — she strongly insists, with a kind of gentle violence of persuasion, for Paul and his companions to stay with her. Similarly, in Luke 24:29, the disciples 'urged him' to stay with them after the resurrection, as if they could not bear for Jesus to leave.
G3849.origine: The word is composed of παρα- (para, 'beside') and βιάζομαι (biazomai, 'to use force', 'to compel'). The basic idea is to force something insistently, bypassing obstacles. In Hebrew, Genesis 19:9 and other passages use the verb פָּצַר (patsar, to press, to insist) to express the same notion — that of an insistence that does not let go.
G3849.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In both occurrences, it describes affectionate and pleading insistence: Lydia in Acts 16:15 urges Paul and his companions to stay with her after her baptism; the disciples in Luke 24:29 urge Jesus to stay with them before he disappears. In both cases, the meaning is not violent or imperious, but rather that of an urgent request, almost imploring, towards someone they do not want to leave. It is a word that expresses urgency and attachment in human relationships.
G3849.portee: This word shows us the tenderness with which the early Christians welcomed Jesus and the apostles. Lydia desires to keep the messengers of the Gospel; the disciples, after the resurrection, plead with the Lord not to leave them. It is a picture of sincere love and attachment to the person of Christ and his message. For the believer, it reminds us that the relationship with God is not a cold obligation, but a heartfelt attachment that makes us desire the presence of the Lord.

sens: A comparison, a parallel of two things
A comparison, an act of comparing
An illustration, an analogy by which an abstract truth is made visible
In Jesus' teaching: a story or image drawn from nature or human life, intended to teach a spiritual truth
By extension: an enigmatic saying, a proverb, a figurative statement
G3850.detail:
1. A parable begins as a comparison: two realities are placed side by side to examine them together. This is the primary image of the Greek word, formed from 'to place beside'.

2. In logic and rhetoric, it is the very act of comparing two things to illuminate one from the other — as when one says 'it is like...'.

3. The parable becomes a developed comparison, an illustration that makes the unseen tangible: Hebrews 9:9 speaks of the Tabernacle as a 'figure', an image of the coming heavenly sanctuary.

4. In Jesus' teaching, the parable takes on a very precise meaning: it is a short story or image drawn from daily life — a sower, a lost sheep, a prodigal son — that both conceals and reveals a spiritual truth. Matthew 13:3 presents Jesus speaking in parables 'about many things': he tells stories, he compares, and those who have ears to hear discover the mystery of the Kingdom.

5. The word is also used to denote a cryptic saying or a proverb: in Luke 4:23, Jesus says 'Physician, heal yourself', which the Segond translates as a parable — a figurative statement that needs interpretation.
G3850.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb 'to place beside': 'para' (beside) and 'ballein' (to throw, to place). Thus, it conveys the idea of juxtaposition. In biblical Hebrew, the word mashal (מָשַׁל) — which Greek translators rendered with this term — originally meant a comparison, then a proverb or riddle, and finally an allegorical story or a proper parable. Jesus revived this rich and ancient form of teaching with vivid images from nature and the Palestinian rural world.
G3850.emploi: The parable appears 48 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in the three Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke). Jesus uses it as his characteristic teaching method: Matthew 13:34 states that he 'spoke to the people in parables', while Matthew 13:10 shows his disciples asking him why he speaks in parables. The disciples receive the hidden interpretation (Matthew 13:36), while the crowd hears the story without always understanding it (Matthew 13:13). The parables cover various themes: judgment (Matthew 21:33-45), prayer (Luke 18:1), the Kingdom (Matthew 13:24, 31, 33), forgiveness and mercy (Luke 15:3). There is only one occurrence in Hebrews (9:9, 11:19), where the word designates a figure or a theological illustration rather than a narrative parable.
G3850.portee: The parable is the pedagogical instrument that Jesus chose to transform the passive teacher into an active reader: it disturbs, it astonishes, it invites reflection. For the Christian disciple, it reveals that one does not receive the truth of the Kingdom passively, but by entering into the narrative, questioning, and allowing oneself to be challenged. It also shows that God speaks the language of ordinary life — seeds, lost children, meals — so that everyone can hear him.

G3851.fr: to expose one's life to danger
sens: To put one's life at risk, to risk dying for a cause
To voluntarily offer oneself to a mortal danger
To sacrifice one's existence to accomplish a mission
G3851.detail:
1. The verb depicts the action of someone who exposes themselves to death. It is a deliberate and courageous gesture: one does not accidentally fall into danger, one throws oneself into it to serve a cause that is worth it. In Philippians 2:30, Epaphroditus 'exposed his life' in serving the Church, ready to die to accomplish the work of Christ.
2. This risk is not recklessness, but an act of love and devotion. The word emphasizes personal sacrifice: giving one's life, not just one's money or time. It is the pinnacle of Christian service — going so far as to risk death for others, like Epaphroditus who nearly lost his life.
G3851.origine: The word is formed from the prefix 'para' (beside, beyond) and 'bolè' (to throw, to project): literally 'to throw oneself forward' or 'to put oneself in front of danger'. It is a military and athletic image: one throws oneself in front of the enemy or peril. The Greek word παραβάλλομαι appears in the books of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 14:38) in the sense of 'to expose oneself to battle'; the form παραβουλεύομαι is a variant of it.
G3851.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:30. Paul uses it to praise Epaphroditus, this messenger of the Church of Philippi who traveled to Rome to be with the apostle, falling ill along the way and nearly dying. Paul emphasizes that this man voluntarily risked his life to serve the Church and the Gospel. The context shows that this word designates the highest degree of Christian devotion, comparable to the love that Jesus himself showed by surrendering to death.
G3851.portee: This verb challenges us about the cost of Christian service. Epaphroditus did not gamble with his life out of fanaticism or bad luck, but out of love for his brothers and for the Gospel. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that living faith may require the ultimate sacrifice, and that those who give everything for Christ deserve our gratitude and admiration. It is a call not to spare one's life when the love of God demands it.

sens: Instruction or order given by an authority
Directive or precept transmitted to someone
Imposed obligation, formal prohibition
Principle or rule that guides action
G3852.detail:
1. A commandment is an instruction or order issued by someone in authority: it is something made known to others for them to execute. In Acts 16:24, the jailer receives an order to throw the prisoners inside the prison; it is a concrete directive to be put into practice immediately.
2. More broadly, it is a directive or precept transmitted, a rule given to guide conduct. Paul writes to the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 4:2) the precepts he has given them on behalf of the Lord Jesus: these are principles of Christian living that must be retained and followed.
3. The word can also designate a solemn prohibition or interdiction: when the apostles are asked (Acts 5:28) if they have not been "forbidden" to teach in the name of Jesus, it refers to a negative order, a prohibition issued by authority.
4. Finally, in the pastoral epistles, "commandment" takes on the meaning of fundamental principle or rule that gives meaning to action: God's commandment in Timothy (1 Timothy 1:5 and 1:18) is an ethical objective: to produce love and the good fight of faith.
G3852.origine: The word comes from παραγγέλλω (paraggellô), "to make known alongside," composed of "para" (beside, near) and "aggellô" (to announce, report). The basic image is that of a word transmitted from one person to another, of someone speaking alongside, who reports a message. The word thus naturally designates an instruction passed from an authority to those who must execute it. In classical Greek (in Xenophon and Polybius), it often refers to military orders.
G3852.emploi: This word appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in Acts and Paul's epistles to Timothy and the Thessalonians. In Acts, it signifies the concrete order given by a civil or religious authority (the order given to the jailer, the prohibition made to the apostles). In the pastoral epistles and to Thessalonica, it takes on a moral and spiritual significance: it is the instruction or rule that Paul transmits as an apostle of Christ, aimed at building up the faith and love of the churches. The word thus designates both the specific order to be executed and the permanent principle that guides Christian life.
G3852.portee: The word "commandment" reminds us that the Christian life is not a solitary or improvised path, but one that follows clear directions given by God and transmitted by His apostles. Understanding what a biblical commandment is helps the Christian distinguish between a mere suggestion and a moral or spiritual requirement. It also recognizes that obedience to God's principles is not slavery, but the path to true freedom and love.

sens: Transmit a message, an instruction
Order, command with authority
Prohibit, expressly forbid
Strongly recommend, urge
G3853.detail:
1. To transmit a message or instruction to someone: it is to give a directive that is passed from one person to another. Jesus, sending His disciples, "recommends" that they go only to the Israelites (Matthew 10:5).
2. To order with authority, impose a command: the one who speaks demands obedience. Paul commands the unclean spirit to come out of the possessed woman (Acts 16:18), or recommends certain things to Timothy (1 Timothy 4:11).
3. To prohibit, expressly forbid: it is to recommend the opposite, in the negative. The authorities in Jerusalem forbid the apostles to speak in the name of Jesus (Acts 4:18); Jesus commands the leper not to tell anyone (Luke 5:14).
4. To strongly recommend, urge insistently: to ask strongly without necessarily obliging. Paul recommends to the Thessalonians what they should do (2 Thessalonians 3:4), encouraging them rather than forcing them.
G3853.origine: The word comes from two parts: "para" (beside, near) and "aggellō" (to announce, report a message). The starting image is that of a messenger bringing a word from one side to the other — a transmission of authoritative message. In Hebrew, this verb often translates "to hear" (שׁמע) in the intensive form, but also verbs of order or command. The family includes "angel" (who brings a message) and "gospel" (good news brought).
G3853.emploi: This verb appears 31 times in the New Testament, concentrated in Acts, Paul's epistles, and the Gospel of Luke. It expresses the authority of Jesus (who commands demons and the sick), that of the apostles (who transmit the decisions of the Church), and that of Paul (who gives his directives to the communities). The word can mean an absolute order ("forbid"), a command ("order"), or a strong exhortation ("recommend"), depending on the context and the seriousness of the situation. The meanings vary depending on whether the action is accompanied by a negation ("do not do") or expresses an urgent request rather than a strict obligation.
G3853.portee: This word shows how the apostolic Church functions: through the transmission of a word of authority, whether that of the risen Jesus, the apostles, or the elders. It invites the Christian reader to recognize true spiritual leaders — those who speak in the name of the Lord — and to listen to their directives. It is also a reminder that the Christian faith is not a private matter: it is lived in community under the guidance of those whom God has established.

sens: Be present with someone, stand by their side
Come to a place, make an appearance there
Present oneself before a person or assembly
Occur, appear suddenly or unexpectedly
G3854.detail:
1. To be present with someone, to support or assist them: it is the idea of standing beside. In 2 Timothy 4:16, Paul writes, "At my first defense, no one stood by me," using this word to say that no one was there to support him at the trial.

2. To come to a place, to arrive after a journey: this is the most frequent meaning in Acts and the Gospels. The Magi "arrived in Jerusalem" (Matthew 2:1), the apostles "arrived in Jerusalem" after their journey (Acts 15:4). The verb emphasizes the completion of the journey.

3. To present oneself before a person or assembly, to show oneself in public: it is to "arrive" before someone for a meeting. Jesus "appeared" at the baptism (Matthew 3:1), John the Baptist "appeared" preaching (Luke 12:51). It is also to rush for a specific action: the accusers "came" before the governor (Acts 23:35).

4. To occur, to arrive as an event or situation: the chief priests "came" against Jesus, meaning they rushed upon him (Luke 22:52). The word can express a sudden or dramatic arrival.
G3854.origine: The Greek word comes from "para" (beside, near) and "ginomai" (to become, to arrive). Literally: "to become beside," hence "to present oneself, to arrive." The corresponding Hebrew in the Greek Old Testament is often "ba" (בּוא), which means "to enter, to come." The preposition "para" adds the idea of being "nearby" or "available," enriching the simple "arrive" with a nuance of active presence.
G3854.emploi: This verb appears 38 times in the New Testament, especially in Acts and the Gospels. It often describes the arrivals of the apostles and messengers in various places: in Jerusalem, in Antioch, before authorities. In Acts, it reports the arrival of missionary travelers (Acts 13:14, 17:10). In the Gospels, it describes the arrival of Jesus at baptism (Matthew 3:1), that of His disciples with Him (Luke 8:19), or the appearance of crowds (Luke 14:21). The meaning can vary slightly: simple arrival, public or official arrival, or hostile arrival. It is a narrative term that propels the action.
G3854.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of the importance of "presence" and "availability." When someone "arrives," it emphasizes that they are now there for a reason, a meeting, an action. This can encourage being present for others, just as Jesus was present. It is also a word of the missionary movement: the apostles "arrive" to preach the Gospel, embodying the commission to go to all nations.

sens: To move from one place to another, to cross a space
To go beyond, to surpass someone or something
To momentarily present oneself before someone
To disappear, to leave, to cease to exist
G3855.detail:
1. The most common meaning describes a physical movement: going from one place to another by crossing a space. Jesus "passes" along the Sea of Galilee (Mark 1:16) and sees the fishermen at work; he "passes" through a village (John 9:1) where he meets a blind man.
2. The word can also mean to surpass, to leave behind. When Jesus "passes" by blind men who are begging him, he moves beyond them until they draw his attention (Matthew 20:30).
3. Sometimes it simply denotes being present, passing by: a "bystander" (someone who passes by) is requisitioned to carry Jesus' cross (Mark 15:21).
4. In a figurative sense, the word expresses disappearance or change: the realities of this world "pass" away (1 Corinthians 7:31), or darkness "passes" when light comes (1 John 2:8).
G3855.origine: The word is composed of "para" (beside, near) and "ago" (to lead, to bring). The basic idea is therefore "to lead beside" or "to lead in front of." The Greek word often translates the Hebrew verb "avar" which also means to pass, to cross, to leave. This composition shows the sense of movement: one passes near something or someone, moving ahead of them.
G3855.emploi: The word appears eleven times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Gospels (nine occurrences). It primarily describes concrete movements of Jesus: he passes along the sea, crosses villages, moves from one place to another, crossed by blind men who implore him (Matthew, Mark, John). The meaning sharpens according to the context: sometimes it is the simple act of passing near someone, sometimes the act of disappearing from view. In Paul and John, it takes on a more spiritual and metaphorical meaning: what "passes" is what is not lasting (1 Corinthians 7:31), what fades before a new reality (1 John 2:8, 2:17). The word never carries a pejorative value; it is a neutral verb of movement.
G3855.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus does not pass by randomly: he passes before those who need him, he traverses places to meet hearts. It also invites the reader to meditate on the ephemeral nature of this world and its pleasures, which "pass away," while those who do the will of God endure. It is an invitation to seek what remains beyond what will vanish.

sens: To publicly show someone as an example to confound or dishonor them
To cover someone with shame by subjecting them to public contempt
G3856.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to put forward as an example," but a negative example: one exposes someone to the eyes of all to ridicule, to confound, to designate them to the shame of the community. It is to publicly display the guilt or unworthiness of a person, as one would display a guilty person in the stocks. In Hebrews 6:6, believers who deny Christ somehow put him on display before the universe, exposing him to disgrace: it is to say that they treat him worse than a criminal exposed to derision.
2. In a figurative sense, it is to cover someone with shame and irredeemable disgrace. The word carries the idea of solemn and unremitting humiliation: not only to shame someone, but to mark them, to consign them to the lasting contempt of all.
G3856.origine: The Greek word is formed from παρά ("beside," "in front") and δείκνυμι ("to show"), hence the idea of "showing before everyone." Latin rendered it as exemplum ("example"), but ancient Hebrew had similar verbs to express the idea of putting forward to confound. The suffix -ίζω gives the verb its strength: it is truly to "make an example of" someone, treating them as a living and visible example of shame.
G3856.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 6:6, in one of the most serious contexts of Scripture: that of believers who "crucify again the Son of God." The author uses this verb to emphasize that rejecting Christ after having known him is not only to deny him in secret, but to publicly deliver him to spectacle and derision—as if one were putting him to death a second time before the eyes of the world. It is a verb of absolute rupture and betrayal, marking the extent of the offense.
G3856.portee: This word reminds us that deliberately rejecting Christ after having known him is not a simple personal doubt: it is to treat him with the most public and grave contempt. It invites the reader to measure the stakes of faithfulness—each act of apostasy is a form of betrayal that desecrates the Redeemer. It is also a call to persevere in faith, so as not to be among those who humiliate the Son of God in this way.

sens: A garden planted with trees and flowers, an orchard or landscaped park
The dwelling place of the soul after death, a place of heavenly bliss
G3857.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a cultivated garden, an orchard or a carefully landscaped park — this is the sense it held in ancient Persian among kings. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses it to refer to the Garden of Eden that God planted at the beginning, but also for other biblical gardens. It is an image of fertility and human order.

2. In the New Testament, "paradise" refers to the place where God welcomes the souls of the righteous dead. Jesus assures the repentant thief: "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43). Paul speaks of having been "caught up to paradise" (2 Corinthians 12:4) — a mystical experience of heaven. Revelation invites the overcomer to eat "from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" (Revelation 2:7). It is the blessed presence of God after death.
G3857.origine: The word comes from the Persian *pairidaeza*, which literally meant "enclosure" or "royal park." The Greeks borrowed it to designate the grand gardens and landscaped parks of the Persian kings — symbols of luxury and order. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew *gan* (garden) and *eden* (delight), evoking the original garden of Genesis. The word has thus shifted from the image of the earthly garden to that of the heavenly abode of the blessed.
G3857.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to refer to heaven or the dwelling place of blessed souls. Jesus uses it on the cross, speaking to the thief of the cross about paradise as the place where he will meet him that very day (Luke 23:43) — a promise of immediate communion with him in death. Paul speaks of it as a mystical experience, a being caught up to heaven where he hears ineffable words (2 Corinthians 12:4). Finally, Revelation promises to the one who perseveres in faith access to the tree of life that is in the paradise of God (Revelation 2:7) — the eternal happiness regained. The meaning thus sharpens: from the earthly garden to the heaven of God.
G3857.portee: This word speaks to Christian hope. For the disciple who listens to Jesus, it says that death is not the final failure, but the passage to eternal communion with God. It is a word of comfort for the one who suffers and believes: the beyond is not darkness, but presence and joy. It also invites to a faithful and victorious life, seeking even now what lasts beyond, the reward that God prepares for those who persevere.

sens: To welcome someone favorably, to admit them into a group or community
To accept something, to give one's assent
To recognize someone as one's own, to approve them
G3858.detail:
1. To receive someone means to welcome them favorably and recognize them as a member of a group. In Acts 15:4, the believers in Jerusalem "receive" the delegates from Antioch, which means to officially welcome them into the community of apostles and elders.
2. To accept or admit something means to take it as true, to recognize it as valid. When Peter "receives" the word in Mark 4:20, he welcomes it into his heart and allows it to bear fruit. Refusing to "receive" pagan customs (Acts 16:21) means not admitting them as legitimate.
3. To receive a testimony or an accusation means to listen to it and validate it. In 1 Timothy 5:19, one must not receive an accusation against an elder without solid evidence: this means not admitting it, not allowing it to count. In a deeper sense, "to recognize" in Hebrews 12:6 means that the Lord receives (admits and approves) those whom He disciplines as His true children.
G3858.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "para" (beside, near) and "dechomai" (to receive, to welcome). This composition reinforces the idea of an active and personal reception: one receives someone or something beside oneself, one admits them. It is a verb from the family of words related to "reception" in ancient Greek. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates notably the Hebrew "nasa" (to bear, to support, to accept) and "ratsa" (to will, to approve).
G3858.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, always in the sense of admitting, welcoming, or recognizing. In Acts, it denotes official reception (15:4), acceptance of practices (16:21), and approval of a testimony (22:18). In the Epistle to Timothy, it refers to receiving a judicial accusation (5:19). In Hebrews 12:6, the religious sense is affirmed: God "recognizes" those He loves by disciplining them. Mark 4:20 shows the reception of the Word itself. The verb always implies a conscious action, a form of assent or approval.
G3858.portee: This word invites us to consider what we truly receive in our spiritual life. Receiving the Word of God is not letting it slide over us, but welcoming it within us and allowing it to bear fruit (Mark 4:20). It also speaks of discernment: recognizing whom we welcome into our community, which doctrines we admit, and verifying before judging. Finally, it reveals divine tenderness: God recognizes His children by correcting them, for true discipline is a form of love.

sens: Sterile quarrel without foundation
Verbal exchange where mutual irritation occurs without seeking the truth
Debate arising from pride rather than the desire to understand
G3859.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a type of quarrel or discussion that goes in circles, producing nothing solid or useful: one opposes, contradicts, but does not advance. In 1 Timothy 6:5, Paul calls "vain discussions" the debates stirred up by false teachers who pervert the Gospel for personal gain.
2. The underlying image is one of friction, mutual irritation — like two surfaces rubbing against each other without resulting in anything. This is why the word characterizes exchanges where each defends their ego rather than seeking the truth together: there is heat, emotion, but no light.
3. Paul implicitly opposes this vain discussion to sound teaching, based on faith and the fear of God. The vanity of the debate lies in its detachment from divine truth: one speaks for the sake of speaking, one quibbles to shine, one contests for the sake of contesting.
G3859.origine: The word is composed of three roots: "para" (beside, near), "dia" (through), and "tribē" (friction, wear). The image is one of mutual rubbing, an abrasion that wears down without building up. The root "tribē" expresses the irritation produced by friction — hence the sense of a sterile quarrel, an exchange where one wears each other down. It is a rare word, coined by Christians to describe a specific evil: theological chatter serving pride.
G3859.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:5. Paul uses it to criticize religious disputes stirred up by false teachers who pervert the Gospel for personal gain. He classifies these "vain discussions" among the fruits of spiritual corruption: one who deceives themselves by believing that godliness leads to gain sows around them endless quarrels, pointless debates. The context shows that Paul is not speaking of simple theological differences of opinion, but of the moral and intellectual deterioration caused by the love of money.
G3859.portee: This word invites Christians to discern between healthy debate — where one seeks together to understand God's will — and vain discussion, which serves pride and divides the assembly. It warns against the danger of turning faith into a pretext for quarrels, verbal jousts, or intellectual displays. By keeping their heart attached to the truth and humble, the believer can avoid these sterile irritations and contribute to the edification of the body of Christ.

sens: to hand over something or someone to another person
to entrust someone to the care or protection of another person
to put someone in the hands of justice, to bring them to trial or prison
to orally transmit a doctrine, words, or traditions
to abandon or let go of someone or something
G3860.detail:
1. In its simplest sense, deliver means to hand over, to pass something from one hand to another. Jesus says to his disciples: "All things have been delivered to me by my Father" (Matthew 11:27), meaning that the Father has entrusted him with total authority.
2. Deliver can also mean to entrust someone to the responsibility of another — like a prison guard receiving a prisoner. In Acts 28:17, Paul explains: "I was delivered from there into the hands of the Romans," meaning handed over to their custody.
3. In the accounts of the Passion, deliver takes on a judicial tone: it is to hand someone over to the authorities for them to judge or punish. Jesus warns his disciples: "They will deliver you up to councils" (Mark 13:9), exposing them to legal prosecution.
4. Deliver can mean to transmit teaching or traditions from mouth to ear. Paul writes: "I delivered to you first of all that which I also received" (1 Corinthians 11:2), speaking of the faithful transmission of the Gospel.
5. Finally, deliver expresses the idea of letting go, abandoning — especially when there is betrayal or malice. Judas who "delivers" Jesus (Matthew 26:16) betrays him and hands him over to his enemies.
G3860.origine: The Greek word comes from para ("beside," "toward") and didōmi ("to give"). The basic image is that of passing something from one side to another, of handing over directly. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates the verb natan ("to give"). This word belongs to the family of Greek verbs of transmission: it is also found in words that speak of receiving what has been handed over, or of keeping what has been entrusted. The preposition "para" adds the idea of passage or transfer from one person to another.
G3860.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the New Testament (118 occurrences) and plays a central role in the story of the Passion. Matthew and Mark use "deliver" primarily to describe how Jesus was brought before his judges (Matthew 26:16, Mark 14:11, etc.), but also how the disciples will be persecuted and handed over to the authorities (Matthew 10:17, Mark 13:9). In the Lord's teaching, the verb takes on a calm and benevolent meaning: "All things have been delivered to me" (Matthew 11:27, Luke 10:22). Paul uses it for the transmission of faith (1 Corinthians 11:2, 15:2) and for the theological image of the delivery of Christ (Romans 4:25, 8:32). The verb changes meaning according to the context: it can be tragic (the betrayal of Judas), judicial (the handing over to courts), pedagogical (the transmission of teaching), or theological (the offering of Christ).
G3860.portee: This word traverses the entire history of salvation in Jesus. It reminds Christians that Jesus chose to be delivered into the hands of his enemies for our redemption — an image of love and sacrifice (Romans 8:32). At the same time, the verb warns disciples that following Jesus means being "delivered" to persecution; it is a call to faithfulness in the face of trials. Finally, the use of the word for the transmission of faith ("what you have received, deliver it") invites the believer to faithfully pass on the Gospel received from previous generations.

sens: That which is contrary to expectation, to habit, to what one believes possible
That which surprises, which deeply astonishes
That which provokes admiration mixed with fear
G3861.detail:
1. The word designates what goes against received opinion, what does not correspond to what one imagined: in Luke 5:26, the witnesses of the miracle of the paralysis see Jesus command the sick man to rise and walk, and they call this "strange things" because only God could perform such an act.
2. It is something that provokes astonishment and sacred fear: the spectators are filled with fear precisely because they understand that they are witnessing something extraordinary, which surpasses the normal laws of nature.
3. The word evokes religious admiration before an act that only God can do: when the disciples and the crowd realize that a mere man claims to forgive sins and heal a paralytic, they recognize there the divine power manifested on earth.
G3861.origine: The word comes from two parts: "para" (against, beside) and "doxa" (opinion, what is believed). A paradoxical thing is therefore "against common opinion" — it surprises because it contradicts our expectations. In Greek, this word emphasizes the incredible, wonderful, extraordinary nature of the event.
G3861.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 5:26. It is at the moment when Jesus heals the paralytic after forgiving his sins. The people around are witnesses to an act that defies all natural explanation: how can a man command the paralytic to walk and be obeyed immediately? This corresponds to nothing they have ever seen. The word thus applies to the miracles of Jesus as they contradict the normal order of things and reveal a superhuman power.
G3861.portee: This word reminds us that faith in Jesus is based on the experience of the extraordinary: it is not an abstract philosophy, but the confrontation with acts that only God can accomplish. For the believer, this invites seeing the biblical miracles not as a simple break in the laws of nature, but as a revelation of who Jesus truly is — the Lord who has the power to forgive and to heal.

sens: Transmission of something from one person to another, from one generation to the next
Set of doctrines or practices transmitted orally rather than in writing
Among the Jews, oral laws and interpretations developed by the ancient rabbis
Teaching received and faithfully preserved
G3862.detail:
1. Tradition is primarily an act: to transmit something, to pass it from one hand to another, from one time to another. This is the meaning of the verb from which this word derives, which means "to deliver" or "to hand over."
2. Among the Jews at the time of Jesus, tradition refers to the oral teachings accumulated over the centuries — interpretations of the law of Moses, rules of purity, religious practices — transmitted by the elders and teachers. In Mark 7:3-5, the Pharisees criticize Jesus' disciples for not following "the tradition of the elders" regarding handwashing before meals.
3. Jesus criticizes this tradition not because it is transmitted orally, but because it sometimes contradicts the word of God itself. In Matthew 15:6, he denounces how one can "nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition."
4. Paul uses the word in a broader sense to refer to any received teaching: in 1 Corinthians 11:2, he praises the Corinthians for holding on to the "instructions" he gave them; in 2 Thessalonians 2:15, he urges them to "hold fast to the traditions" they received from him.
G3862.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb παραδίδωμι (paradídômi), composed of παρά (para-, "beside, alongside") and δίδωμι (dídômi, "to give"). The image is that of passing something to someone, entrusting it to them. Tradition is therefore what is transmitted, what passes from hand to hand through generations. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew נָתַן (natan, "to give") and derives from the fundamental idea of transmission.
G3862.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the New Testament. Its usage is mainly concentrated in the Gospels (Matthew and Mark) and in Paul's epistles. In the Gospels, Jesus and his critics discuss the "traditions of the elders" — practices of the Pharisees and scribes that are not found in the written Law of Moses. Jesus does not oppose tradition itself, but its abuse: when it conflicts with God's commandments. In Paul, the word takes on a different tone: there is nothing pejorative about "holding fast to the traditions" one has received (1 Corinthians 11:2, 2 Thessalonians 2:15). Paul also calls the Corinthians to reject the "traditions of men" that lead them away from Christ (Colossians 2:8).
G3862.portee: Understanding biblical tradition requires discernment: there is a living apostolic tradition that is faithful to the Gospel, which must be kept and transmitted (as Paul urges in 2 Thessalonians 2:15). But there are also human traditions that stifle the word of God or divert from Christ. The Christian must test every tradition in the light of Scripture: it is only valuable if it serves and illuminates it, never if it contradicts or replaces it.

sens: To provoke in someone a feeling of envy, rivalry, or resentment
To inspire jealousy by inciting the desire to compete
To awaken vigilance or zeal through competition
G3863.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to provoke jealousy as a feeling of envy: to create in someone the desire to possess or equal what another has or does. In Romans 10:19, Moses announces that God will provoke the jealousy of Israel by offering salvation to a nation that is unworthy — the idea is that this jealous rivalry should push Israel not to be surpassed by the Gentiles.
2. More broadly, it is to incite a feeling of rivalry or resentment that drives to action. Paul states in Romans 11:11 and 11:14 that he hopes to provoke the jealousy of the unbelieving Jews by announcing the salvation of the Gentiles, so that they react with zeal and desire to regain their privileged position.
3. By extension, it means to provoke a reaction of vigilance or even irritation in someone. In 1 Corinthians 10:22, Paul asks if Christians want to "provoke the jealousy of the Lord" — that is, to put Him in a position to defend His honor and holiness against those who defy Him.
G3863.origine: The word is composed of the prefix παρα- (para, "beside," "against") and the verb ζηλόω (zēloō, "to rival," "to envy"). This verb itself comes from ζῆλος (zêlos, "zeal," "jealousy," "rivalry"). The etymological meaning is therefore: "to incite jealousy in the face of something." In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew verb קָנָא (qanâ, "to be jealous") in the intensive form, which evokes a passion of ownership or rivalry.
G3863.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, all in Paul's epistles. It is used in Romans 10:19 to quote Moses' promise: God wants to awaken the jealousy of Israel towards the salvation offered to the nations. Paul revisits this theme in Romans 11:11 and 11:14 to explain his missionary strategy: by announcing salvation to the Gentiles, he hopes to provoke the jealousy of the Jews and lead them to seek their own salvation. In 1 Corinthians 10:22, the word takes on a more serious tone: it is about not provoking divine jealousy, that is, God's indignation towards those who transgress His covenant. Thus, the word navigates between human psychology (envy, rivalry) and theology (God's passionate reaction to unfaithfulness).
G3863.portee: This word reveals a subtle divine strategy: God can use envy and rivalry as engines of repentance. Paul shows that jealousy — this supposedly lowly feeling — can become a pathway to salvation if it drives people to seek what others possess: the grace of God. For the Christian, this invites reflection on jealousy: is it mere carnal envy, or can it be a sign that one truly desires what matters? It also reminds us that one cannot provoke the jealousy of the Lord without consequence through unfaithfulness.

sens: Located at the edge of the sea
Along the shoreline
G3864.detail:
1. The word designates a geographical location situated directly at the edge of the sea, on the shore. It is an adjective that describes the position of a city or region in relation to the water. Capernaum, where Jesus comes to settle after Nazareth, is thus characterized as being "near the sea" — referring to the Sea of Galilee, which the Gospel also calls a "lake."
2. The image evokes a territory that runs along the coast, directly exposed to the waters. It emphasizes the geographical accessibility of the place and its relationship to the maritime and commercial world.
G3864.origine: The Greek word results from the combination of two roots: "para" (beside, next to) and "thalassa" (the sea). This composition is classic in Greek for describing the position of an object or place in relation to another. It is an adjective formed to express the proximity of the shore.
G3864.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 4:13, where it characterizes Capernaum. After leaving Nazareth, Jesus settles in this city described as "near the sea." This geographical detail anchors the Gospel story in a real setting and situates Capernaum as a strategic center, accessible by both sea and land, where Jesus will begin His public ministry in Galilee.
G3864.portee: This term helps the reader visualize the concrete context of Jesus' life: it is not an abstract teaching, but rooted in a precise and inhabitable geography. Capernaum, an active coastal city, becomes the seat of Jesus' Galilean ministry, highlighting that the incarnation of Jesus unfolds in the real world, in places that people frequent.

sens: Laisser de côté, passer sous silence
Oublier volontairement ou involontairement
Traiter avec indifférence ou manque d'attention
G3865.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to leave something aside, not to look at it properly, to ignore it. This is the basic idea: when one looks elsewhere, one no longer sees what was in front of them. In Acts 6:1, the Greek widows of the early Christians were 'neglected' due to an inequitable daily distribution of aid: they were not forgotten intentionally, but left behind due to insufficient attention.
2. From this comes the meaning of not giving something the attention it deserves. It is a lack of care, an omission: one passes by the problem without addressing it. This lack of fairness in the distribution of aid to the widows created tension between two groups of believers.
3. The word can also suggest contempt or indifference: treating someone or something as if it does not matter. Here, it was certainly not a deliberate contempt, but the result was that some widows felt excluded.
G3865.origine: The Greek word is composed of 'para' (beside) and 'theōreō' (to look at, to examine). The image is one of looking aside, leaving something in one's field of vision without focusing on it or addressing it. Thus, it is first examining without really seeing, then not caring about it.
G3865.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:1. It is precisely there that the complaint of the Hellenists (the Greek-speaking Jewish Christians) against the Hebrews (those speaking Aramaic) is recounted: in the daily distribution of material aid to the widows, some Greek widows went unnoticed or were in the background. This problem prompted the apostles to better organize the service of the deacons. The context shows that it is a practical neglect, not malice, but it was nonetheless real and a source of tension.
G3865.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that practical justice and attention to the weakest are not details: neglecting widows, the poor, or strangers is failing in love for one's neighbor. It also shows how the early Christians were able to correct these shortcomings by instituting a dedicated service. It is a lesson in vigilance: it is not enough to want to do good; we must also examine our actions so that no one is forgotten.

sens: Bien confié à quelqu'un pour le garder et en prendre soin
Confiance placée en quelqu'un
Enseignement reçu et à transmettre fidèlement
G3866.detail:
1. A deposit is primarily a good, wealth, or a precious object entrusted to someone else for safekeeping and protection. It is like leaving something of value in the hands of a trustworthy person.

2. By extension, it is also the trust itself that one places in someone — the certainty that they will watch over what is dear to us. Paul says in 2 Timothy 1:12 that he is 'persuaded that he [God] is able to keep [his] deposit,' meaning his life and soul entrusted to God.

3. In Paul, the word mainly refers to the teaching of the Gospel received and to be kept carefully for transmission to future generations. Timothy is instructed to keep the 'good deposit' (2 Timothy 1:14) by avoiding false doctrines — it is a spiritual treasure to defend.
G3866.origine: The Greek word παραθήκη comes from the verb παρατίθημι (to place beside, to entrust). The prefix παρα (beside) and the root θη (to place) give the image of something that is placed 'in the hands of' someone. It is exactly the Hebrew word פִּקָּדוֹן (piqadon) from the Old Testament, which describes a deposit entrusted according to the Law (Leviticus 6:2). The word is active in Paul: it is not passivity, but a charge that one receives and is responsible for.
G3866.emploi: Paul uses this word three times, all in Timothy — his disciple in whom he invests the future of the Church. In 1 Timothy 6:20, the deposit is the sound teaching that must be kept against 'vain and profane babblings.' In 2 Timothy 1:12 and 1:14, the word is enriched: it refers not only to doctrine but also to the Christian's life and faith, entrusted to God and to be preserved by the Holy Spirit. The context of persecution ('I suffer these things') shows that keeping the deposit means remaining faithful to the faith at all costs.
G3866.portee: This word reminds the Christian that he is not the owner of the faith — it is a deposit received from God and from generations before him. Keeping the deposit means refusing compromises and false doctrines to transmit the Word of God intact. It is also a beautiful image: we can entrust our lives to God, certain that He will keep it precious, like a trustworthy treasurer.

sens: Conseiller fortement quelqu'un, l'inciter à agir ou à penser d'une certaine manière
Avertir, mettre en garde contre un danger ou une mauvaise action
G3867.detail:
1. To exhort is to give urgent advice, with authority and conviction: one does not timidly ask, but actively encourages someone to do something or adopt a certain attitude. In Acts 27:22, Paul exhorts his shipmates to take courage in the face of the impending shipwreck: he does not simply say 'take courage,' he strongly urges them toward this attitude of trust.
2. The word can also mean to warn or advise in order to avoid harm. The exhortation then focuses on the warning: it emphasizes the danger and engages the person to turn away from it. This aspect appears in Acts 27:9, where the context suggests advice given to avoid peril: the sailing season becomes dangerous, and the advice aims to prevent catastrophe.
G3867.origine: The Greek word paraineō is formed from para ('beside,' marking the idea of proximity and accompaniment) and aineō, a rare verb meaning 'to praise' or 'to speak well of.' Exhortation is thus literally 'speaking in favor': one stands beside someone and speaks to encourage and guide them. This combination of accompaniment and persuasive speech reflects well the action of exhorting: it is not a cold order, but a warm and engaging counsel.
G3867.emploi: The verb paraineō appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 27, during Paul's maritime journey to Rome. In Acts 27:9, it is used in the passive or with a similar sense ('the season had passed'), suggesting advice given previously. In Acts 27:22, Paul uses it in the first person to actively exhort: he addresses the 276 people on the ship in the midst of a storm, urging them not to lose hope. In these two occurrences, the word carries the idea of advice or warning given in a crisis situation marked by doubt, fear, or uncertainty.
G3867.portee: Exhortation reveals Paul's pastoral heart: in the face of danger, he does not keep his confidence to himself; he communicates it. It shows us that one who has faith must not only believe but also encourage others to believe. It is a call for the Christian not to remain passive in the face of others' discouragement but to gently urge them toward trust in God, especially in trials.

sens: To ask something of someone, to request them to do or give something.
To beg someone not to do something, to implore them to refrain.
To politely decline an invitation or request, to excuse oneself for being unable to respond.
To firmly reject something, to push it away.
G3868.detail:
1. In Mark 15:6, the word refers to the act of asking: the crowd "asks" for a prisoner from the governor, soliciting him to release him. It is a request directed to someone else.
2. In Hebrews 12:19, it is the opposite: it pleads that one should not speak to him any further. It is to beg someone not to do something, or to refrain from an action.
3. At the wedding in Luke 14:18-19, the guests "excuse" themselves: they politely refuse the invitation by giving a reason. They ask to be excused from coming, apologizing to the master.
4. In 1 Timothy 4:7 and 5:11, Paul says to "reject" or "refuse"—the profane tales, the young widows. It is a categorical rejection, a clear and unambiguous refusal.
G3868.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "para" (beyond, beside) and "aiteomai" (to ask, to pray). The primary idea is to ask that something be set aside, or to pray someone to keep their distance. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "bakash" (to seek, to ask). The meaning has nuanced from simply "to ask" to "to refuse," as to refuse is in a sense to "ask that something not be done."
G3868.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. In Mark 15:6, it means "to ask, to solicit." In Luke 14:18-19, all the guests "excuse" themselves one after another: the context is that of a courteous refusal of an invitation. In 1 Timothy 4:7, 5:11, and Titus 3:10, Paul uses it to order to "reject" or "refuse"—a heresy, young widows, a divisive man. In Acts 25:11 and Hebrews 12:25, Paul and the author say not to refuse something: they commit instead to accept it. The meaning thus oscillates between "to ask" and "to refuse," but always with the idea of taking distance or putting an end to something.
G3868.portee: This word helps the believer understand how to discern what to welcome and what to set aside. Paul teaches to refuse false teachings and temptations, while committing not to refuse God's calls—even difficult ones like suffering. It is a lesson in discernment: knowing how to say no to what distances one from faith, and yes to what God asks.

sens: to sit next to someone
to listen attentively by placing oneself near someone
G3869.detail:
1. The word describes the physical action of sitting near a person, in their company. It is a simple yet significant gesture: one voluntarily places oneself next to someone to be in their presence. In Luke 10:39, Mary chooses to sit at the Lord's feet to not leave him and remain in his proximity.

2. Beyond the simple act of sitting, the word evokes attentive listening and communion. When one sits beside someone, especially at their feet, one adopts the attitude of a disciple receiving their teaching. Luke 10:39 shows Mary who, by sitting at Jesus' feet, actively listens to him and gives him her full attention.
G3869.origine: The word comes from the combination of "para" (beside, near) and "kathizō" (to sit, to be seated). The image is of someone taking position by placing themselves close to a person, to be near them. This same root is found in many words that express proximity: "to be with," "to stay beside." In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the verb "yashav" (to dwell, to sit) to express this idea of presence and stability.
G3869.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:39, in the famous scene of Martha and Mary. Mary sits beside Jesus to listen to his teaching, while Martha is busy with household tasks. This unique usage is enough to show the importance of the gesture: to sit beside Jesus is to choose to prioritize his presence and his word over any other activity.
G3869.portee: This word reminds the Christian that communion with the Lord requires a deliberate choice: to sit beside him is to take time to listen to him, to abandon distractions and concerns to focus on his word. It is an invitation to prayer, meditation, and intimacy with God, like Mary who chose "the better part."

sens: To call someone to oneself, to summon or invoke them
To beg, to earnestly pray someone to grant a favor
To encourage, to strengthen someone in a trial or decision
To comfort someone in sorrow or pain
To warn, to admonish with authority and kindness
G3870.detail:
1. To call someone to oneself means to summon or invoke them: it is the act of bringing someone or imploring them. In Acts 28:20, Paul "calls" the leaders of the Jews to plead his case.
2. To beg someone is to pray with insistence and humility to obtain grace. A leper "begs" Jesus to touch him (Mark 1:40); Paul "begs" the Lord three times (2 Corinthians 12:8); it is the tone of urgent need.
3. To encourage and strengthen means to bolster someone's determination or courage. Jesus "exhorts" his disciples to have faith (Mark 5:36); Paul "exhorts" the converts in Lystra to remain in faith (Acts 14:22).
4. To comfort is to soothe someone's sorrow by comforting them. Rachel in mourning "will not be comforted" (Matthew 2:18); Jesus promises to comfort those who mourn (Matthew 5:4).
5. To admonish is to warn firmly but in a kindly spirit. Paul "exhorts" the Romans to present their bodies and souls to God (Romans 12:1); it is a loving warning.
G3870.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition "para" (beside) and the verb "kaleō" (to call). The starting image is thus "to call to oneself." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it mainly renders the verb "naham," which means both "to be moved with compassion" and "to change one's mind." This broad range of meanings—from simple calling to deep consolation—can be explained by this common root: someone who calls you "to themselves" places you in their presence, where they can comfort, exhort, or beg you.
G3870.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the New Testament (over 100 occurrences) and appears mainly in Acts, Paul's epistles, and the Gospel of Luke. Its primary meaning varies according to the context. It first denotes prayer (Mark 1:40: the leper begs Jesus), then pastoral exhortation (1 Corinthians 1:10: Paul "exhorts" to unity; Romans 12:1: moral exhortation). It also expresses consolation (2 Corinthians 1:4: God comforts in affliction) and encouragement (Acts 14:22: Barnabas and Paul "exhort" the disciples). In Acts, it often describes kind persuasion (Acts 16:39: the magistrates come to "appease" the apostles). The tone varies: to beg is humble, to exhort is firm, to comfort is compassionate.
G3870.portee: This word reveals how God and his servants deal with souls: not by force or threat, but by calling, prayer, loving exhortation, and consolation. It shows that the Christian faith is transmitted and strengthened through kind words. For the believer, "parakaleō" suggests that we can both confidently beg God (he "calls us to himself") and be exhorted, comforted, and strengthened by our brothers. It is the language of the Spirit of the Lord, called "Paraclete"—the one who is sent "to us" to help us.

sens: To cover something by placing something in front of it
To make imperceptible, hidden from view
Figuratively: to make incomprehensible, obscure
G3871.detail:
1. In its literal sense, the word means to cover something by placing a veil or screen in front of it: it's like putting a curtain in front of a window so that what is behind cannot be seen. The particle "para" (beside) reinforces the idea of hiding by placing something to the side or in front.

2. By extension, it means to make something invisible or imperceptible, to conceal it from sight. The meaning shifts from the concrete (putting a physical veil) to the abstract (removing clarity from something).

3. In a figurative sense, used in the New Testament, the word means to make incomprehensible or obscure, preventing the perception of the real meaning. In Luke 9:45, Jesus' words are "veiled" to the disciples: they do not seem clear to them, the meaning is hidden from their understanding, "so that they might not understand it." This is a divine misunderstanding, which temporarily protects them from a truth that is too difficult before the resurrection.
G3871.origine: The word is composed of "para" (beside, in front of) and "kaluptô" (to cover, to veil). The root "kaluptô" refers to the action of covering with a veil or cloth. In biblical Hebrew, a similar idea is found in the words "pachad" (fear, something hidden) and "alam" (to hide in the causative form), which express both the idea of hiding and making obscure. This verb belongs to the family of words related to concealment and obscuration in New Testament Greek.
G3871.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 9:45. It is in a context where Jesus has just spoken of his death and resurrection. The disciples do not grasp his words, and the Gospel explains that "the word was veiled to them." This is not simple ignorance: it is a voluntary veiling of meaning, a mystery from which God temporarily protects them "so that they might not understand it." After the resurrection, this veil will be lifted and they will fully understand what Jesus had said. This is the only use of this compound verb, while the simple verb "kaluptô" (to cover) is more common in the Scriptures.
G3871.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage reveals that our misunderstanding of God's words is not always a fault on our part: it can be voluntary and protective. God sometimes veils the complete understanding of a truth because we are not yet ready to receive it. It is an invitation to humbly accept the moments when we do not grasp everything, trusting that God will reveal its meaning at the right time.
